before: Of the Creator, for He is a support; and still, the removal of a number from Him makes a dyad, as it is evident that the three came by addition. But to humans, those things which are signified by the two, if a calculation were added, no longer remain material or human, partaking of rectitude; for it is not necessary merely to act, but also with right reason, so that it may receive praise.

And one is able, by changing the mode of speech, to take these things toward the perfection of the soul; for first a passion must come to the soul, then thus a disposition must become, and thus to impel toward action. And we say a passion is not the thing being denied, but the impulse of the soul as it would imprint upon the virtuous; and these things also happen from the opposite.

Three, therefore, are these offspring of the diligent; let the pre-passion now be a burden in relation to indifferent matters. And if one, imposing [them] even upon interpretations, might find something useful, let him observe. Shem, indeed, is interpreted perfect, Japheth breadth or beauty, but Ham is daring or impetuous or heat or excess.

And what other offspring would have been fitting for the righteous, such as perfection, breadth and beauty, which are all the marks of virtue? For beauty, joined with breadth, makes the wide road go outward, which leads to destruction; but if it is that Ham is interpreted daring or impetuous or heat or excess, let these be taken as domestic to his manner, as if toward the worthless son for a reproach, but for the perfect, let them be received with careful use; for the virtuous is most unforced, since even the violent seize the kingdom; but such a one is also daring against the opposing powers, according to Paul the blessed saying, 'Our struggle is not against blood and flesh' (Eph 6:12), and the following: this impetuous one, just as he is daring, is not acquiring impetuousness toward evil, but happening upon virtue, being hot and zealous in the Spirit, from which he also stands apart from human [things] (Eph 1:11–12).
But the earth was against the Lord, and the earth was filled with injustice. And the Lord God saw the earth, and it was corrupted, because all flesh had corrupted his way upon the earth.

The corruption of the earth does not signify the loss of the so-beautiful element into non-existence, but rather the excess of the sins of men; the earth calls men by a metonymic manner, just as the psalmist says: 'Let all the earth worship you and sing to you' (Ps 66:5), and again 'Sing to the Lord, all the earth' (Ps 96:1); for when it is said 'The heavens and the earth were finished' (Gen 2:4), this element is signified, and 'Let the earth blossom' (Isa 45:18). Such has become the wickedness of men, who are called earth, as to see God, that element which incites them through much goodness and the great things of the wings. For it has been said: 'If, Lord, you observe iniquity, Lord, who will stand?' (Job 35:12). It does not bring wrath day by day, but when the moderate measures of sins occur, as it was said just as in the prophet Jonah: 'The cry of wickedness ascended to God' (Jon 2:2), and concerning Sodom: 'The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has filled [the heavens], and their sins are exceedingly great' (Gen 18:20), just as here the similar is said: 'And the earth was filled with injustice' (Gen 6:11), and the rest.

See that [God] is not previously ignorant, but is manifesting the watchful power toward vengeance, just as in 'And God saw the earth, and it was corrupted' (Gen 6:11). And he calls the corruption the wickedness and the punishment upon it, just as the Scripture often declares in that which was said by Paul: 'If anyone destroys the temple of God, God will destroy him' (1 Cor 3:17); for he who, sinning through lawlessness, works the corruption of the temple of God, is found under punishment and is destroyed, the punishment being now signified by the corruption. And it is a corruption also to be delivered over to an unproven mind; for this is the most extreme punishment. And it is not necessary, according to the Manichaeans, to suppose that useless matter remaining in the wandering...

before: Because all things have come to be, this number is taken up for the sake of order and for the sake of harmony, as has been said; and because of this, due to our weakness and our inability to perceive otherwise in any suitable way. Let what is said be clear from an example. Our body possesses color and size together with its substance, and it did not come into being as separate things divided in time, but rather, except by thought, the one is before and the other is after.

In the same way, the world, having come into being in order, is completed not by time but by harmony. For no part of the world will be able to be conceived in relation to the others unless the rest exists. And the luminaries, having come into being on the fourth day, show by their preciousness that they were spoken into existence in this way because of the reason concerning them. For the tetrad, being in power, exists as a ten in honor; for through all Scripture, the ten is praised.

But that a certain number, if it is signified in the divine letters, does not always declare a multitude, but a reason, it is to be understood from what has been said concerning God: 'I have left behind seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal' (1 Kings 19:18). For if such a number was the case, the prophet would not have said, 'I am left alone' (1 Kings 19:10), nor did they have the pure relationship toward one another; for they were not fleeing themselves.

A precious reason concerning the seven—for this is both without seed and without fruit—submits the thought that the saints are of the same power, even if they exist as humans, having established something divine and being considered superhuman through contemplation and life. But also in the Apocalypse, John, saying that twelve thousand men fall to the Lamb, who is the Savior, and these virgins with women not defiled, shows that there is a certain precious reason concerning this number; for no one would have said such a great multitude of virgins were gathered from those who believed while John was still alive, perhaps even if there were not so many of them.

We say therefore that the world has come to be in six because of the previously mentioned reason, and the luminaries on the fourth because of the previously mentioned [reason], that the tetrad, being a ten in power, possesses the honor. Another of their work is to be for signs; for the stars and the sun himself signify many things; but they signify not as making, but as revealing. And those proposing fate set them as poets, saying that if this does to that, but not so, but so that they might signify seasons, months, years; it is not the signifying that is poetic.

For he says, 'And let them be for signs and for seasons and for years' (Genesis 1:14), which signifies the annual seasons, the spring, the winter, and the others; for being in this climate the sun does this or that. before: Dogs, according to what was said: 'Watch out for the dogs'; and having fully received the craftiness of wickedness, they were dissolved in a manner fitting the destruction caused by wickedness, this being a symbolic indication of the water. These themselves are also earthly, as having lost the heavenly image; and they themselves perished 'upon the dry land,' of a wickedness possessing nothing life-giving (Gen 7:23–24).

And Noah alone was left remaining, and those with him in the ark, and the water rose upon the earth for one hundred and fifty days. Fittingly Noah is saved without participating in wickedness, along with those who were with him and being instructed by him, having risen above the weight of the water understood allegorically by fifteen cubits, reaching the temple through the steps, and having fulfilled the things foretold through the number: for 'water' 'will not be able to much extinguish love' (Song of Solomon 8:7).

And God remembered Noah and all the beasts and all the livestock and all the winged creatures, as many as were with him inside the ark. And God brought a wind upon the earth, and the water subsided; and the fountains of the abyss were covered and the cataracts of the heaven, and the rain was restrained from the heaven. And the water was receding as it went from the earth, the water was receding and retreating after fifty and one hundred days.

And the 'remembered' is to be heard in a God-befitting way, not as from forgetfulness, but just as he says concerning the ungodly: 'I do not know where you are from; depart, workers of iniquity; never did I know you' (Matt 25:12), the 'never' here indicating knowledge, 'never as having had you as our own'; 'remembered' is not having been overlooked—for the holy is before God always—but rather to make the memory of him a beginning of a race to lead him to the beginning, and similarly for the others. Some seek where the water of the deluge has retreated, through the coming of a wind, by which the water was subsided, whether this be the will of God or a divine power being at work; and in addition to this, it became a co-worker for the subsiding of the abysses and the upper downpour being hindered (Gen 8:4).
And the ark rested in the seventh month, and the following. The spoken is manifest; let us look at the thing toward understanding.

Yes, the ark is the church saving those who are clinging to it through prudence and works of virtue, which also sits in highness. For it never becomes in lowliness, therefore nor do the gates of Hades prevail against it; it stands before Christ glorious, having neither wrinkle nor line or anything of that kind, since even Christ is in highness, which is shown in 'Behold, this one comes leaping upon the mountains' (Song of Solomon 2:8), the prophets and Moses and the invisible powers. It sits, therefore, upon the rock, by the word of the cleavage of piety. For 'the foundations' (Psalm 127:1) of God are 'in the holy mountains' (Psalm 127:1), which also are the city of God; for 'God' (Psalm 89:2) 'established it for all eternity' (Psalm 89:2). 'For they received' (Isaiah 26:2) it says 'the city having the foundations' (Isaiah 26:2), of which God is the craftsman and creator. Let the mountains also have driven away 1380 sheep that did not fall by the plan. And if anyone through the number wishes to speak technically, he might say that the stability of the divine church is shown through it; for this is square, and the same is also a cube; for three times three is twenty-seven. And 'Arariad' is interpreted as a testimony of descent; but God testifies to that which is upon the church through a descending polity, which is unseasonable; for it has been said: 'If you pass through water, rivers shall not overwhelm you' (Isaiah 43:2), and again: 'We passed through fire and water, and you brought us out to refreshment' (Isaiah 43:2). And it is also good that the deluge be fulfilled in a year; for when the true sun shines and illuminates our intellect, then every disturbance of the soul shall be driven away.

before: By the greatness of the light that has come, God would see the whole analogy and the harmony it has with other things. We say of the painter that he sees differently through art, even though he also receives it through sensory perception. For the one practicing art, seeing the analogy, perceives the beauty of this member in relation to that and this in relation to that, whereas the non-artist does not reach this appearance, which comes through calculation and technical intellect.

before: Every person, having been cut off from the truth, is drawn into various kinds of wickedness. And regarding those traveling, many are the upward paths, but one is the straight one.

Thus the waters were scattered, which we have set down to be the rational judgments being diverse and being carried by disposition. Therefore, the one who benefits from them by knowing them wants them to become one, since he is also their creator. For it is said that he is the maker of their essence, but each is his own according to the diversity of his judgment.

Therefore God himself protects so that these things might be gathered into one assembly, so that they might become such a water, which is that above the heavens, being one not by number but by harmony. Immediately also, a single soul and heart of all the believers becomes one, not by number but by harmony and by the same purpose and by striving for a single end.

Therefore the God of all things protects so that the divided things might be brought into harmony; for this is the intention of the beneficent God. Since they were poured together and were moving irregularly according to judgment, they are first gathered into assemblies. And it is not contrary to the one protecting to say that they were gathered into their assemblies, God saying: 'Let the water be gathered into one assembly' (Genesis 7:7); for they will not yet have reached the limit of the utmost virtue, the gathering before this being fitting.

And just as if someone, wanting to train his child in perfect matters, entrusts him to a teacher, if he were to first lay these characters before him, then, having grasped them, he would proceed not contrary to the one who entrusted him; for in this way he will reach the perfect things from these. And again, if a king, protecting a city under himself, commands to prepare those by which the construction of the city might happen, he does nothing other than what is the command; for from these and through these the construction will be fulfilled.

So also the rational judgments, being in wickedness, were not able to reach the final desired end, unless various progresses became, which are the systems of the waters; for after the progress, he protects them to come into one assembly. Therefore that which happens does not fight against the command, but...

But this command, as it is at the perfection of the order, is a kind of economy pre-arranging the logical things in which they were able, so that they might thus reach the end. And it happened thus, and the water was gathered into its assemblies. The intention of God is to gather the scattered into one—for he says this—but they, remaining until the end in their own assemblies, were gathered, which are progress.

And God called the dry land, and the collections of the waters he called seas (Gen 1:10). Just as we were saying that the earth, existing after heaven in the beginning, had this name and the heaven had this name, but after the heaven and the earth existing in the beginning, the expanse is primarily called so, but by appellation heaven; so also the earth existing after the heaven existing in the beginning is called this, but concerning which it is now said, this is called by name dry, but by appellation land: 'God called the dry land' (Gen 1:10), as it has been said; 'He called the expanse heaven' (Gen 1:8).

Regarding the allegory, God calls the dry land not by granting it a new name, but because he commanded that the waters lying upon it, which were kin to the abyss, be separated, he calls it dry—for it has been said: 'And let the dry appear' (Gen 1:9)—so that it might truly be called land, having remained as its own underlying soul, and being set free by God for the reception of seeds, it might bring forth a hundred, sixty, thirty of divine, perfect fruit. For the kind of fruit which, upon the being-cultivated earth, the more ready one brings forth... or the later one, contrary to the care of the farmer or the nature of the earth, so also regarding souls: some, having received the seed, stifled it by anxieties and cares, but those having used the agriculture most excellently, having been trained to such an extent, as to benefit themselves and to stand as a source of benefit to others. For the difference of plants is manifold and varied, and the hand that works is irregular, being used such that it will more clearly demonstrate the dryness of the evil earth.

before: The phrase 'everyone who killed Cain' is said instead of a vocative, instead of 'O Cain, everyone who killed', or other ways about him, so that it might be 'everyone who killed Cain', which some say would not be a sin for certain powers. To these same things he gave a 'sign' 'not to let him be killed' (Gen 4:15), which was God's command for him; for no such judgments happen without forgiveness.

He set a sign, the momentum of repentance after the falls, by which he will not be easy to take away. For it is a great good not to fall; but to come after the falls into recognition would be a second chance, which God provides through teaching to prevent falling into deception. Such a mind is suggested by what is said in the Psalms: 'Light was signaled in the face of the Son, or the light of your face toward us, O Lord' (Ps 89:13), which you say properly, speaking of divine thought. For so also the fleeing from the face of the bow would happen, of the face of God in us, as it is said, while it exists; and what follows confirms it: 'So that your beloved ones may be delivered' (Ps 100:2). Therefore, through philanthropy and goodness, God gives a place of repentance even to those falling greatly, so that a recovery of virtue may happen again.

So Cain went out from the face of God and dwelt in the land of Nod opposite Eden (Gen 4:16). We say that the going out of Cain from the face of God is not to be taken locally, but that everyone sinning becomes outside God, since we also understand entering toward God in this way, the Psalmist saying: 'Enter before Him in gladness' (Ps 100:2); For someone enters before God, leaving all things outside—sins and sensible things—and becoming another in the world, so that he might thus become a partaker of the knowledge concerning God. It is said here therefore: 'Cain went out from the face of God' (Gen 4:16), and we do not say that...

What kind of place is it in which God exists, and from which Cain, while existing, went out? For God is uncircumscribable and is not subject to places, even if a temple has later become a teaching for symbolic worship. Cain went out, having made himself unworthy of the face of God, having become otherwise thoughtless.

Concerning such things it is said, 'God is not before him' (Ps 31:9), and concerning the sons of Eli it is said, 'The sons of Eli did not know the Lord' (1 Sam 2:12); for if they drew near to the temple, it was in their disposition and works that he was found outside. That Cain went out in this way, the following shows: 'And he dwelt' (Gen 4:16) for he says 'in the land of Nod, opposite Eden.' For 'Nod' is interpreted as 'trembling'; for where was it necessary for the one departing from peaceful virtue to dwell, except in 'trembling,' in an unstable and uncertain thing, which is wickedness? And also 'opposite'; for wickedness is contrary to virtue.

We must remember, therefore, that when we were participating in the account of Adam's expulsion, we noted that He expelled him not as one having gone out of his own accord, but still possessing an impulse of longing for the enjoyment of the luxury of Paradise; therefore, opposite these things, He settled him, just as He himself had managed the dwelling. For to those who do not sin greatly, since virtue does not exist within them deeply, a certain quick opportunity is given, indicating a return, being given toward God, which was not said of Cain.

For neither has he been settled nor expelled, having perished through a willing longing for evil; therefore he dwells in 'trembling,' being incessantly disturbed, since he desired this, of the contrary stable thing, in order to have a strong standing, as if he could stand even with God, according to what was said: 'But you shall stand with me' (Ps 16:8), and by the Savior regarding those not tasting death: 'There are some standing here' (John 12:35), who were his acquaintances. But even Paul, exhorting not...

before: Noting that the word was becoming certain as something to come to pass, he was implying that it is not proper to remain in the things before it, thereby dishonoring virtue.

Sarah said: 'I am wronged by you; I gave my maidservant of mine into your bosom; but seeing that she has conception in her womb, I have been dishonored in opposition to her; may God judge between me and you.' (Gen 16:2). The 'from you' is twofold, that is, either 'from you' or 'from whom'; so that regarding the 'from you' it is thus: when anyone, desiring to use the preliminary exercises for the sake of virtue and the perfection of wisdom, remains in these in some way dishonoring the virtue by not using them for what is necessary, and the 'from whom' will receive the same intellect, the only difference being that he truly dishonors the virtue by hastening to give birth from the introduction alone and setting this as the end.

Pay attention also to 'in opposition to her'; for the virtue was not simply dishonored, but 'in opposition to her'; for when anyone, having used the preliminary exercises because of the perfection of wisdom, goes beyond the need, he dishonors the virtue in himself. As for 'may God judge between me and you', one might say it literally as having been spoken because of some movement from a human being in her, but following the intention of those who have understood, it is said toward the one remaining in the introductory character: that you did not bear perfect children from me, but rather allowed them to remain still in those things.

Abram said to Sarah: 'Behold, your maidservant is in your hands; use her as it is pleasing to you.' (Gen 16:6). Regarding the literal sense, the word of the patriarch introduces an indifference, as he receives the maidservant from the woman without desiring pleasure and now being content with her and withdrawing when he wishes; but toward an elevation, the diligent one, even if remaining in the introduction and being alienated from the perfection of virtue, receives the rebuke from her unpleasantly, and then, having moved from the smaller things, as if subjecting himself to her, uses her instructions to restore authority. For whenever he is eager to say, do, and think all things toward the goal of virtue, he most readily receives the corrections from her.

And Sarah mistreated her and drove her away from her presence. This mistreatment of the handmaid, whom we lead into the preliminary exercises, turns out to be a kind of dismissal of them. For those who are pressing toward perfection no longer need them. Because of this, she rightly departs; for she no longer endures the introductory elements of having attained progress and perfection.

And an angel of the Lord of God found her at the water spring in the desert, at the spring on the road to Shur (Gen 16:7). And the angel of the Lord said to her, 'Hagar, handmaid of Sarah, whence do you come and whither are you going?' And she said, 'I am fleeing from the presence of Sarah, my mistress' (Gen 16:8). From these things, one can see and know the virtue of Hagar and that she was not ungrateful, as an angel was conversing with her and placing care for her not as a trivial matter; for it is evident that it was according to the will of God. It was not unlikely that she was diligent, as she was chosen by the holy Sarah for the companionship of Abraham. And her thankfulness is shown by her saying, 'I am fleeing from the presence of Sarah, my mistress'; nothing trivial is said about her. In the things previously mentioned, Sarah's virtue and the spiritual understanding of the divine Scriptures were placed, while Hagar was the introductory and shadowy one.

Therefore, the one approaching the divine instruction ought to attend to her in this way, so as to understand him according to letter and spirit, in a manner and order that fits. Thus it is necessary for the child of Sarah's introduction, so that he may reach the more perfect things, just as it was said concerning the Israelites, 'that they were first entrusted with the words of God' (Rom 3:2), which are given until a time of correction. For no one remaining in the letter or in her introductory wisdom is being made an opponent. Therefore, this lover of wisdom, if he remains using only the introductory things, in a way dishonors virtue; and if he rises up, he will have lost the introductory guidance as having departed from it; once progress has been attained, the former things pass away, just as was the case with the Egyptian Hagar; for the things of the introduction are confirmed by earthly examples.

before: Above all things the end is evident: that for which the tent has been pitched, having advanced through progress and remaining toward perfection, and for which the one persuaded by the word, despite being dissuaded, will arrive: 'Watch your foot, lest when you go into the house of God and draw near, you hear' (Ps 119:10). For thus he will be able to dwell in the house, saying, 'That I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days' (Ps 27:4). It must be known that through these things the divine citizenship is symbolically shown, even if the persona of Abraham is not yet fully completed, for he has not yet been called away.

And he pitches the tent 'by the sea,' being firm and unshakeable because of holding fast to virtue perfectly, so as to say: 'Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?' (Rom 8:35) and the following, regarding which he says 'sea,' would not be sins. For whenever a saint is, even in perfection, he has a dizziness pressing upon him and the instability of created nature, which the perfect man, as a charioteer, prevents from the activity of evil by remaining in its power, which is blessed; for this is good even while existing in virtue, since even the evil man exists in the power of virtue, having turned to this by his own intention, though he did not guard himself as one who has become good.

And he himself also pitches the tent 'in winds from the south' in a way suitable to reaching the mountain of the house of God and being illuminated through all things from the east, which are the virtues according to their kind, and making no care for any of the opposing things—for even the waves from the sea do not overturn his well-established structure—which transforms the words of Jesus into works by becoming a feast; for this is interpreted as 'winds.' For the great feast is the perfection of virtue. For this is also what the psalmist says: 'Hear the voice of rejoicing and confession of those celebrating' (Ps 100:1); for he who rejoices at the presence of the Spirit and confesses, not as one sinning and repenting, but as one giving thanks, celebrates—for the name of confession lies in place of thanksgiving, as in 'We confess to You, O Lord Father of the heavens...'

before: Not a mountain, but the house of God; for this is interpreted as Bethel, which is not only [a house] but also with other things according to what was said in Aisma: 'My brother is like a deer or a young hart upon the mountains of Bethel' (Gen 25:9). For many mountains and hills are in the house of God, as from 'Behold, this one comes leaping upon the mountains, fleeing upon the hills' (Ps 42:6); and with each progress there is to ascend to a hill, and from the hill to a mountain, and from lower mountains to higher ones; for this is known both in the introductions of virtues and in the virtues themselves.

But there is one mountain above all, the Savior and Lord of us, concerning whom it is said: 'The mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest at the latter end of the days' (Zech 14:4), which is another thing compared to the other mountains, so as to speak for the sake of the holy teaching, so that no one might misunderstand: 'Why do you suppose [it is] fortified mountains?' Then, teaching the most excellent mountain, he says: 'The mountain of God, a fertile mountain, a fortified mountain, a fertile mountain. Why do you suppose [it is] fortified mountains, the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell?' which signifies the Lord having become man. For the incarnation is shown through this word, just as also with Job: 'Did you not care for me like milk, and did you not curdle me like cheese?' (Job 10:10). For the Savior alone [comes] from a virgin; therefore it is said. Is this said concerning others? For no one else had such a constitution. Therefore Job did not say 'I was curdled,' but 'You curdled me like cheese'; for what the Spirit has done, the casting of the seed in others works by the command of God. And the same 'fertile' exists from the presence of the Spirit and from the power of the Most High.

And in the common sense, all and even the temple of the Savior are by creation from God, but [the Savior is] exceptional through the Lord; for He has used it as an instrument toward the incarnation. And just as all the earth of God is a creation, but the temple had [it] exceptional because of the God being honored there, so also regarding the things previously mentioned. And since, wherever God honors, that place is called His house, Jacob testifies saying: 'How fearful is this place! This is nothing else but the house of God, and this is a gate of heaven' (Gen 28:17). Therefore one must not pay attention, if [he] says...

Many will call themselves Christs according to what is said: 'Many will come in my name, saying, I am the Christ' (Matthew 24:5). For there is a mountain in which God pleased to dwell; for the pleasure of the dwelling was not made by any man. Therefore, Abram, advancing through the intellect, burns toward this mountain.

Indeed, coming without neglect, he testified to him, saying: 'Your father Abraham rejoiced in order to see my day, and he saw and rejoiced' (John 8:56), having been enlightened by the true light being presented to him from the preceding advancements. And it is also good to say that this mountain is 'toward the east'; for it has lights from every side. Whatever conception of this mountain you take, it is luminous; for it is called wisdom, word, life, truth, justice, sanctification, and redemption. All these things, while rising, are lights—not many lights according to their essence, for they have one underlying subject, the Son of God—but diverse according to their energies.

Therefore, 'toward the east' of the house of God, which shines through all, the holy man came, being led by virtues; and it is also possible to call the various doctrines of piety 'eastings,' through which Abraham had arrived at the tent, which he used for the advancements—for this tent signifies the house of God being permanent; for 'I will pass through a place of wondrous habitation until the house of God' (Psalm 84:10). Having passed through the tent, he presses into the house that remains forever, with which there is no other ascent. This is also said in another psalm: 'How beloved are your habitations, Lord of powers! My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 84:2).

For he who has not yet reached the courts, while in the tents, has love advancing and expects completion in saying: 'My heart and my flesh shall rejoice in a living God' (Psalm 36:9), when it occurs in that establishment, with which there is no other, into which those who have reached are called blessed, the psalmist saying: 'Blessed are all those dwelling in your house' (Psalm 84:4), not as sojourners but as dwellers; for this belongs to those in tents and advancements, but to dwell is to come into the house of God, in which they are blessed, as it were 'unto the ages of ages,' praising him.

before: It is to be noted that he does not speak concerning the sea monsters as 'let the waters bring forth sea monsters' (Gen 1:21), but that he himself has made them. before: Regarding what is said: 'So our soul has passed through the unsubstantial water' (Ps 74:13), which the Benefactor intends to free us from, such a great evil; those who have erroneous thoughts are called winged because they are said to possess meteors, and they seem to think excessively compared to other men, which the Philanthropic God intends to happen outside of this state, so that they might harmonize the understanding, which they undermined regarding things not necessary, into what is fitting and proper according to rational nature, so that they might recover the proper place of the divine fall, from which the deviation occurred.

The evil powers, the devil and his angels, were great sea-monsters according to the rules of allegory, who are called dragons according to the Scripture, meaning that the devil himself is called by this designation much more so. Toward the Savior, indeed, it is said in the manner of a hymn: 'You crushed the heads of the dragon, you crushed the heads of the dragons upon the water' (Ps 74:13). It is clear that these things happened from God, not as they turn out to be trivial, but according to their essential underlying nature. For God did not make a devil or demons as such they are, but they themselves embraced their own destruction; for the Scripture says [of] the angels who did not keep their own rank (Jude 1:6).

before: A tetrad leads to a decad. For the tetrad is a power of ten, as has already been shown; . The foundation, in which the lights are made, must receive faith and perfect virtue, which the psalmist, possessing it, said: 'The Lord became my support' (Ps 18:2). For without the Word it is not possible for the church to be; for this is its support and foundation.

These same lights are signs; according to the literal sense, they sometimes signify a kingdom, or torches, or lightning, or something else of the great things according to their use; but according to anagogical sense, as has been said, they signify progress, and often the desert of the soul; for the lights indicate this allegorically. And God saw that it was good. And he blessed them, until the fifth day.

Since the preceding creation is the mortal animals upon the earth which happen to be for the sake of man, following this, the other animals and plants were made because of his need; for some he takes for food, and others for his healing; and there are others, some having become for the sake of labor, and others for some need of his; for nothing stood in being without purpose. Therefore God says: 'Let the waters bring forth creeping living souls and flying things flying upon the earth.' (Gen 1:20). For it was necessary even these to stand in being for the sake of man. This is therefore explained by the air and heaven being often called expanse. And the 'and it happened thus' is similarly to be understood by those who have perished. And what [is meant by] 'and God made the great sea creatures'?

before: [...of] the fish of the sea and the winged ones of the heaven and the beasts and all the earth and all the creeping things creeping upon the earth. And God made the man; according to the image of God He made him, male and female He made them. And God blessed them, saying: 'Increase and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the winged ones of the heaven and all the beasts and all the earth and all the creeping things creeping upon the earth' (Gen 1:28).

The word 'man' signifies also the composite living thing which is composed of soul and body, and especially the soul. Therefore, the wise Peter the apostle calls the hidden part of the heart 'man', and the blessed Paul: 'For I consent according to the law of God according to the inner man' (Rom 7:22), that is, according to the mind, according to the soul. But when it is said: 'There was a certain man in the land of Assyria' (Gen 45:2), and: 'It happened when many men began to become' (Gen 6:9), it signifies the common [meaning]. If therefore we take the explicit [meaning], the composite man signifies the 'And God said: Let us make man' (Gen 1:26).

And not only regarding the composite, but even regarding the visible and perceptible, that is, the body, the blessed Paul intends to extend the name of man, saying: 'Even if our outward man is being destroyed, but the inward is being renewed day by day' (2 Cor 4:16). And according to a first imposition, each of us was composed of soul and body, but there are those who say that man is composed of three, of soul and body and spirit, which they construct by joining themselves to the apostolic saying which says: 'And the God of peace sanctify you completely, and your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23), not following [the idea] that it must be said concerning the Holy Spirit in order to be whole, which is not even destined to come into weakness. Therefore, they produce another proof from a different saying having this: 'The Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit' (Rom 8:16); for they say our spirit is a different spirit from the Holy Spirit, being witnessed by the Holy Spirit when it is well. And that from Daniel: 'Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord' (Dan 4:35).

They think it is a mere assistant. But those who do not want there to be anything other than the spirit besides the soul say that it signifies the will through the spirit, or that he has shown even the soul by the designation of the spirit. But those renewing this argument say that, having used a connective conjunction, even in 'spirits and souls of the righteous' (cf. Heb 11:35), he shows the soul to be something other than the spirit.

And as a constructive argument for the composition of man from soul and body, they produce that which is said in the Gospel, broken out: 'Do not fear those who kill the body but are not able to kill the soul; but fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell' (Luke 12:4). And if it is the case that men kill one thing and not the other, then the body and the soul are two. We say, therefore, man and the body only, but not simply, but man with an addition; and the soul alone is man not simply, but man within; and the composite is man simply, without anything added.

Let it therefore be sought here concerning what is said regarding God of all things: 'Let us make man according to an image and in our likeness' (Gen 1:26). The man has not become according to an image of God in the composite sense; for God is not man-shaped. And the divine teaching confirms this; for it is said that God is spirit and light (1 John 1:5), and light and spirit do not have the form of man.

But the Scripture also discusses God having seven eyes, seeing all the earth (Rev 4:8), while man has two; so therefore the man will not be found to be according to the image of God in this way of our seeing. But these things we say not as if God has seven sensible eyes, but we are investigating how man is according to the image and likeness of God; for the Word has shown his perfect contemplative power through the seven, and through the virtues which the number seven has, as has already been foretold.

Again, God is said to have wings, just as the holy one says: 'In the shelter of your wings you will protect me' (Ps 17:8); but man is a wingless animal, and the wingless is not able to have the image and likeness of God, not through sensible things received by us, but through intuitions surpassing and carrying those who desire this upward. It must therefore be investigated how man is according to the image and likeness of God.

Since they follow the moving [things] and are joined to the spoken [word], let us take a little regarding this. The day is understood in two ways: according to the chronological interval and according to the illumination of the air around us. For when it is said, 'And on the third day' (Genesis 1:8), the extent of the day is indicated, not whether the day is bright or dark; but when someone says that today is a gloomy day, he does not say this looking at its extent. Therefore, if the divine word says that a first, second, and third day existed before the creation of the sun and the other luminaries, one must look to the extent of the chronological interval, and say to the one questioning the divine writing that seventy-two, as if hours, have come to pass after the creation of the firmament, before the luminaries had come to be, and this is nothing wonderful. For the sun of the day is not a maker of the day but exists as a sign, since even those things constructed mechanically, some would call the measures of the hours not makers but signs. Thus the sun signifies the times...

The sun and the moon do not perform [the action]. However, to signify is different from to do, so that such an incongruous interval was not established from the creation of the sun and the other luminaries; for if there were a significance, it became a distance of three days.

And God said, 'Let the water under the heaven be gathered together unto one place, and let the dry land appear' (Gen 1:9). And let the explicit exposition of the present heading be this: not all water, but the [water] under the heaven, God commands to be gathered into one gathering; for it has been said that the firmament became in the midst of the waters, so that the [part] of the water remained above, and the [part] below. And the utility of the command is shown by saying, 'and let the dry land appear' (Gen 1:9); for the [land] lies hidden by the waters, and thus having [existed] unsuitably, it was [positioned] for the generation of plants and animals. He says, 'And the water was gathered into its gatherings' (Gen 1:10). And one thing, as someone might say, is that which is in the command, but another is that which is in the completion of the work; for it is stated into one gathering that all the water be gathered, and the counter-part says that the water was gathered into its gatherings and thus the dry land appeared.

And the seemingly contradictory thing is restored by the one presiding over the history in this way: the ocean is one sea enclosing the whole inhabited world; for so say those who have reasoned about places, that an island which has a relation to the whole sea—for it is surrounded and enclosed from every side—this, he says, the whole earth and the whole inhabited world has a relation to the ocean. And there are some [parts] of the ocean as if being cast out into deep places, and thus the other seas were formed. If therefore he says, 'into one gathering' (Gen 1:9), he speaks of the universal gathering, which is called...

before: All these things, possessing the ferocity of malice, the devil, called a serpent, is condemned following after all things. And the sentence approaches: 'You shall go upon your belly and upon your dust' (Gen 3:19). For because he thought he had been influenced in his intellect and was deceived into thinking he would have great foods, the word interprets his fall by saying that the earth shall be food to him, having nothing divine or elevated, but being darkened around earthly things, his ruling faculty having fallen, which the breast signifies; he no longer produces something divine or heavenly because of the generative power, which is signified by the belly, having his care around matter and earthly things.

That the belly is thus understood is learned from the opposite, from the singing of the blessed David: 'And your law within my belly' (Ps 119:11), which signifies not the sensible member but the power of the soul. For those who have become men in repentance do not neglect, saying that their intellect, which ought to take divine foods, has been cast down into the earth: 'Our belly has stuck to the earth,' according to all earthly things having happened, to be fed by earth and to give birth to earth. For just as the belly is a vessel of foods, so also it is a workshop of those being formed.

Those producing vile things go crawling upon the earth, but those producing the divine say: 'From the fear of you in the belly we took and labored and brought forth' (alluding to Ps 126:6/Gen 3:16 context); the same offspring of the intellect is also its food. For each thing, in its own way, turning away from the life that is necessary, acquires life for itself.

Similar to this is what was said regarding the rich man: 'You have received your good things in your life' (Luke 16:25), and Lazarus likewise the bad. And observe that regarding the vile one he spoke of his indifferent good things, because he himself considered those very things as good and hoped in them, and for this reason also said 'your good things'; but regarding Lazarus, his own bad things were not spoken of; for not from his own...

You suffered, even if you bore it bravely. And Job, being deprived of pleasant things, since he did not reckon them as his own good, but knowing their nature, as they were given by God, they were used for him, did not say, 'If we had received my goods' (Job 1:21), but 'If we have received goods from the hand of the Lord' (Job 1:21). For he himself considered them goods, the virtues happened to be [his], but for those following, by the judgment of God, indifferent, as it was fitting to be used, sufficient for those in need; so indeed he said: 'My door is open to everyone coming.'

I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed; he shall bruise your head, and you shall bruise his heel (Genesis 3:15). Often indeed, seeing a woman's friendship toward a man occurring with simplicity, from which deception follows, making such people act shamefully, we strive not for a peace of hatred, which is the fruit of the Spirit, but for a turning away of peace, by which the Savior comes to bring a sword, saying: 'I did not come to cast peace, but a sword' (Matt 10:34), dividing and cutting off those desiring to be helped from those attempting to harm. God being good, therefore, plants enmity in those for whom peace and harmony are hostile. For when someone, through ignorance of the evil, falls into it and learns that it is disastrous and harmful, he reaps no small benefit.

Consequently, the seed also makes enmity between seed and seed, and him to her. before: He is consumed by labors, bringing all things to the man more strongly than a master, awaiting the commands issued from him, while the man himself is exhausted by cares, being constantly occupied with toil and sweat throughout his life. For he is not a partaker of those who grieve the woman, but he himself is gripped by peculiar pains throughout his living, laboring and wearing out both body and soul on various things; for his household matters are not the most foolish, such as the upbringing of children, and the many pains of these, whether pressed by diseases or preempted by death, from all of which a surpassing remedy and sufficient labor are needed, and many things could be said which are most manifest to all.

Let us see also each of the things said. To the one it has been said, 'Cursed are you,' but to Adam not so, but 'Cursed is the ground because of your works' (Gen 3:17), and rightly so; for he, not having been defeated by sin, did not surpass it, but followed the woman according to that which was given to us beforehand, 'The woman whom you gave to me' (Gen 2:24), when we were presented with the apostolic saying: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14). But even to the woman directly, threats are given: 'I will greatly multiply your sorrows' (Gen 3:16). And the saying 'You are dust and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19) also brings forth the characteristic of the bodily substance; for the soul does not have its beginning from the earth, so that it might also be dissolved into it, according to those who falsely claim it is corruptible.

Since, as we have seen before, Paradise was taken by us allegorically to be a divine place of enjoyment for the blessed powers, so too the things concerning the man and the woman must be interpreted. We have, therefore, from the blessed Paul, principles leading toward the upward ascent, him saying, 'This is a great mystery, but I speak concerning Christ and the church' (Eph 5:32). The church, therefore, brings forth children in sorrows, for the labor of virtue precedes and works out unremitting repentance toward salvation; and it brings them forth through the bath of regeneration. For labor follows virtue, while pleasure follows ease. The Savior teaches this, saying, 'Narrow is the gate and compressed is the road leading to life' (Matt 7:14), but 'wide' and 'broad is the road...'

[The one] leading to destruction, and many are those entering into it. And the sighing has praise through virtue being produced: of those groaning. But it also has a turning toward the man Christ, being ruled by him, so that according to his pledges, the offspring of virtue being obtained from her might have its perfection through him.

For 'I betrothed to you one man a pure virgin to Christ,' says Paul (2 Cor 11:2). For blessed is the church, when it is surrounded by Christ, and each woman is blessed who is under a perfect and diligent one and a savior of the duty of ruling. For let no one, taking the strayed lifestyles, attempt to counterfeit; let him test the word, for they were not provided for in the divine word concerning such things, and Paul, teaching this, exhorts, saying, 'just as also the Christ [did to the church],' which is self-evident.

And regarding the commandment containing [the rule], as it is not necessary to merely say that the one forbidden to eat in these things was sufficient once having been made clear now, this alone we should pass over, while noting this: that because Adam, having heard the voice of the woman, did not previously sin, but followed her, through which the things said stand; for 'Cursed is the earth in your labors' (Gen 3:17), he says, 'Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth to you' (Gen 3:18). For what from the following of the body is not painful, pleasures and cares being attached to it from it?

For these thorns the Savior interpreted, which entangle the seed being cast by Jesus, if the receiver does not receive into this depth; but also the one called Earth, who receives much rain upon her and brings forth good vegetation for those whom she also cultivates, receives blessing from God; but bearing thorns and thistles, she is unproven and near to a curse, the end of which is into burning. If therefore anyone, through study, should cause these to sprout but does not forgive, he will have a pasture, which is some food; for first the growing thing will be grass-like, as also the Savior says, 'whether an ear of grain' (John 12:24). This, therefore, the spiritual, the diligent one will not find without study nor without toil.

before: Humans are animals of choice, participating in sciences; for they do not live by sensation alone like the irrational, but the virtue of the rational is already shown through being inventors of arts. The first point regarding the literal sense is this; the things regarding the ascent are these.

The cattle-tender is different from the shepherd; for the one grazes with science, but the cattle-tender does not. Abel was the righteous shepherd, governing his irrational powers—the desiring, the appetitive, and the spirited—according to the right reason; but the cattle-tender, lacking science and being a certain pleasure-seeker, is subject to the sensations alone, not ruling them but being ruled by them.

And as a clear example, it would be said in this way: The physician uses touch differently than one looking toward pleasure; this one, then, is a kind of cattle-tender, but the physician is a shepherd, for he uses reason with sensation. In the same way, regarding smell and the other sensations, the one using them with reason is best. For reasoning begins the sensation, and if the reasoning is held in check, the man receives the qualities according to the passions, such as being called a lion through the spirited part, a fox through the cunning, and a serpent through the earthly part, and also being called a horse through the pleasurable part; for they say, 'You have become like mares' (Psalm 55:19), and other men are called such because, being entirely of the sensations, they produce nothing divine, like us; for he says, 'Do not become like a horse and a similar creature, which have no understanding' (Psalm 49:20).

The cattle-tender is such, being a certain base person, not dwelling in a house but in tents, a precarious thing, not imitating those who dwell in tents for the sake of entering into the house, who also say as in the Psalm: 'How lovely are your dwellings, O Lord of hosts: my soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 84:1-2); for the one progressing from tents desires the courts, singing: 'I will go in the way of a wonderful habitation until I reach the house of God' (Psalm 77:13). The other brother is 'he who showed the harp and the lyre' (Psalm 33:2), being his brother in righteousness; for he has neighbors for the enjoyment of pleasures and the deception through music being worked upon the ears; for 'woe' to 'those who rise up...'

Chasing the morning and the evening, remaining blind; for wine will intoxicate them; for they drink wine with lyres and psalteries, but they do not look upon the works of the Lord. And the other [one] crafts war-gear from bronze and iron, the bronze making its sound, just as Paul writes, 'I have become a sounding bronze' (1 Cor 13:1); and he himself is also a worker of iron, being a certain sophist and deceiving through seeming probabilities.

And Lamech said to his wives, Adam and Zillah: 'Hear my voice, women of Lamech; be instructed by my words; for I have killed a man for a wound, and a young man for a bruise' (Gen 4:23-24); for seventy times seven has been avenged from Cain, and from Lamech seventy times seven. I believe that being instructed is brought about only by divine instruction, and it differs from hearing, when it is joined with it; for the one, being instructed, is the hearing of that which is near, but the hearing is the hearing of that which is far off, and the word is not near. And in Isaiah, 'Hear, O heaven, and be instructed, O earth, for the Lord has spoken' (Isa 30:2), is not said in parallel, which is also 'Be instructed, O heaven, and I will speak' (Isa 40:9)—for instead of 'Pay attention,' other interpreters say 'Be instructed'—'and let the earth hear the words from my mouth' (Isa 30:2). And they say such an observation exists: when the law was being given by God, since it happened to be near the heavenly works, for this reason the heaven is commanded to be instructed; but when they departed from the upright citizenship, as to become far from the earth, then it is said, 'Hear, O heaven'—for they happened to be far—'and be instructed, O earth,' for this [earth] was near through its attachments. Therefore Lamech did not say 'Hear' and 'Be instructed' in parallel, but rather we have observed the difference between them in the Scripture not to be untimely; and what is it that we should learn, he says: 'Hear my voice, women of Lamech; be instructed by my words' (Gen 4:23). And someone might say that the voice and the words are in parallel; but he who seeks precision even regarding these would say that regarding the voice he ordered 'Hear,' but regarding the words he ordered the more precise thing, which is to be instructed.

before: He planted a vine, which is the chosen one; for he planted the people to be a kingdom and a chosen priesthood. He built a tower to provide refuge for the approaching enemies (Isa 5:2); the tower is a teaching tool, guarding and at the same time mocking the enemy's onset. Having built, he hears: 'If a spirit of the prevailing one ascends upon you, do not leave your place' (Luke 17:5). He also made a hedge and placed a fence around it, which signifies the safety from the angels. And despite all these things having happened, he remained in the same fruitlessness; therefore he says: 'What more shall I do to my vine when I have done nothing for it?' (Isa 5:4).

I have done all things without fail; therefore, since they themselves do not have the power to say what must happen, I will say, 'I will announce to you what I shall do to my vine' (Isa 5:5-6); I will take away what I gave it, 'I will pull down its wall and it shall be a pavement, and I will take away the fence and it shall be a plunder' (Isa 5:5-6). before: During one of the six days, angels and archangels and all the spiritual essence did not receive a beginning. Regarding what was said in the 82nd [section]: 'The wise will hide perception.' And so that what is said may become clear through an example: perception is the tactile sense of hot and cold, hard and soft, rough and smooth; and to the irrational and the child, these things are manifest through touch. But when the physician comes to feel the pulse, he hides the perception, providing a reason through the movement of the throbbing vessels. In the same way, the laypeople perceive images by sense alone, but the scribes contemplate them with the logic of the eye.

Thus the man, before the transgression, was looking at things with a mind that was scientifically applying understanding to things, as is necessary. As long as he had these eyes directing themselves toward appropriate spectacles, he did not know evil; instead of testing it, he did not accept it. But when these eyes grew dim, and those leaning toward evil were opened, then he also became cast out.

The devil, having this will, seeks to make the woman wise, introducing envy to conceive of God, and promising great things, so that by these things he might entice, saying: 'You shall become like gods, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:5), while also subverting her intention with more views, lest the idolatry through images be joined, all while flattering the angels who are with him.

before: The image-nature is already active within him. Let the saying be clear by way of an example. Man is a rational being; and this essential capacity exists also in the infant, though the rationality does not. Thus the infant also has this power; for when the logos is fulfilled, these things are demonstrated, if he responds to instruction.

So also the image, until it is encroached upon, maintains the value of the first creation; but when evil and hardship are attached, it is necessary to receive the flesh according to what has been said in the Gospel, which is the word of repentance, so that having developed the lying-in-waitness lying upon him, we might make manifest the forms of the image.

And 'and let them rule the fish of the sea and the birds of the heaven and the cattle and all the earth and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth' (Genesis 1:26), according to the previous discourse, would show the beginning [dominion] of man over the animals subjected to him. For one would marvel how all things, being beyond his power and being wild and having a nature to harm, are simultaneously caught by great fires and nets; yet this would not happen in this way, unless he had a beginning [dominion] over them from God. For even when large herds of various animals are driven by the gathering of a child or otherwise by a weak man, they clearly demonstrate that there must be a divine power in the rational animal, by which these things are subjected to him. And a beginning [dominion] is nothing other than a lawful standing. Nothing of the others rules the same-kind; and even if the so-called firstling of a flock is a sheep, it begins the herds according to the preceding way, not by reasoning according to men the shepherds, but it does this by nature. And man became according to the image and likeness of God, in order to rule the things mentioned.

And since we say that the mind of man is man according to another understanding, having been commanded to become according to the image and likeness of God, we appropriately receive that he rules those beasts about which the saint says he sends up a prayer, 'Do not deliver to the beasts a soul confessing to you' (Psalm 22:20), which were the opposing energies, outside of which he prays for the confessing soul to be, or evil thoughts being subjected by them. Regarding Job, it is said: 'Behold, beasts eat grass beside you like oxen' (Job 1:24), not that the immediate beasts were driven wild in nature by Job, but that the disorder of opposing powers was being made manifest because they lacked strength against the greatness of the saint's virtue. And many things are found in the Scripture where animals are mystically led.

For indeed, some are called fishes symbolically among men, whom the cast kingdom of the heavens draws into the sea. For from every kind, that is, from every character of men and nation, the proclamation of the Word draws. So it begins also with these fishes. And the winged ones are intellectual, some being slandered and others praised: 'Young vultures flying on high' is said, and concerning a father or mother being spoken ill of, it has been said: 'Ravens tore him from the cliffs and young eagles devoured him' (1 Kings 19:4), which would not be according to history, since slandering parents is found everywhere, while ravens are not found everywhere; but it is clear that, being held by this error under dark energies, he is in some way subdued and devoured, those which, being lowly, are accustomed to wear away a crevice.

And regarding the others, the lover of beauty will find animals taken both praiseworthily and slanderously. Thus the man has been set as ruler over all these, having been born in the image of God. The apostles, having come to this state so that they might be like God according to the image, were the rulers of the fishes of the intellectual sea, having become fishermen by Christ saying to them: 'Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men' (Matthew 4:19), as also to Peter: 'From now on you will be catching men' (Luke 5:10), those dwelling in the aforementioned sea.

And because they were also rulers of beasts, they received authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy. But it is also shown in the Psalm how authority is given by God to the righteous against such things, the Holy Spirit saying to the virtuous one: 'He shall tread upon the asp and the basilisk; he shall trample the lion and the dragon' (Psalm 91:13). And He gave them also authority over the winged ones who snatch up the one being sent by the Word.

before: They served as parents to the offspring, but the whole was drawn by the guidance of God. It is necessary to take 'through God' more simply instead of 'from God'; for thus also Joseph said, 'Is not their declaration through God?' (Gen 41:56) instead of 'from God.' 'And he added the birthing of the brother of Cain, Abel' (Gen 4:2). Philon indeed intends for them to be twins from a single conception; for, he says, it is appropriate to him who begot Cain to have added the birthing of his brother Abel.

before: He found it rightly, those who do not seek in the way they ought, not finding; for they say, 'They shall seek me,' yet 'evil men and they shall not find' (John 14:20). From this it is known that he sought well from the judgment and gift of God, when, as if sealing the grace himself, he gives: 'Not of the one willing nor of the one running, but of the merciful God' (Romans 3:27), and 'If the Lord builds a house, in vain the builders labored for it' (Psalm 127:1).

Yes, 9. These are the generations of Noah. Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God (Genesis 6:9). The genealogy of the righteous is not so much of men as of virtues; for these are his preceding offspring. This indeed teaches the written Spirit; for it being the case to say the generations of Noah, it brought forward: 'Noah was a righteous man, being perfect in his generation, and he pleased God' (Genesis 6:9).

Let us see what is signified by 'perfect in his generation.' According to a first interpretation, one might say that, compared to the men of his own time who had endowed themselves with immeasurable evil, he was perfect; this is not a great thing, if he were compared to the unknown, for it might perhaps be possible to say that of those entering the ark with him, he was called perfect because he was different; for it is indeed likely that they were such from the holy habit.

It might also be said thus: the generation of the righteous is similarity, and this is signified from 'This is the generation of those seeking him' (Psalm 14:3); for having said, 'Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? He who has innocent hands and is pure in heart' (Psalm 24:3-4) and the following, he brought forward: 'This is the generation of those seeking him,' having spoken of one generation of those adorned with the same virtue. By this, in the opposite way, similarly, it is the thing said: 'Sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in their own generation'; for the generation of such things is the similar state and way of life.

And it is necessary to hear 'perfect' as it is in men, which Paul said to know perfectly in part, saying concerning the perfect: 'When the perfect comes, that which is in part shall be done away' (1 Corinthians 13:10); all the perfection being accomplished in men is as towards that in the future.

An age is complete only in part. Let what is said be clear by way of an example: he who is in the first letters is complete, yet as far as the one listening to grammatical discourse, he is incomplete. And the Apostle himself, saying, 'We know in part and we prophesy in part' (1 Cor 13:9), speaks this concerning himself and those like him: 'As for those who are perfect, we think this,' and 'But we speak wisdom among the perfect' (1 Cor 1:6); for just as the citizenship existing there is incomplete, as we have said, as far as the knowledge that is to come, being 'face to face' (1 Cor 13:12), even if it has reached its utmost limit.

And the things said about Noah—that he was righteous, and perfect, and pleasing to God—must be taken all at once, even if the words have an order; for he was 'righteous' and 'being perfect' he had a pleasingness toward God. But the perfect and the righteous are anticipated by the pleasingness; for it is not that because he pleased, he became righteous and perfect, but because he appeared righteous and perfect, he has been shown to be pleasing to God. And if Noah is said to be a man of such a state, it is not necessary to be surprised, since we have often observed that the name 'man' signifies more; for it is not regarding mere dust alone, as it is said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not acting as men and walking according to man?' (1 Corinthians 3:3), and concerning the devil sowing evil thoughts, it is said: 'A man has done this' (John 6:70); here, in addition to declaring the nature, it also signifies the 'man' as the one who saves according to the 'image' (Gen 1:26). And also, that he 'being perfect pleased God' (Genesis 6:9); for he pleased God having already been promised perfection, not pleasing God by pleasing in everything, but by being [pleasing] to both righteous men and in other ways to men; for he is praised not only for pleasing the righteous, but after [that] for pleasing God.

before: Nevertheless, the promise of the teaching word happens in this way: it will prescribe; for often, through closeness, those teaching know the burdens of those being discipled and do not ignore their intelligence. But that the state of the stomach is unclear is learned from the Gospel, saying of the Savior: 'Woe to those with full bellies and to those nursing at that time' (Luke 10:23). For such conditions are unstable when a trial stands near. Because of this, the word says that such ones desire to be weaned: 'You who have been weaned from milk, who have been turned away from the breast, expect hope upon hope in tribulation upon tribulation'; for as a remainder, standing in stability, they receive tribulation upon tribulation.

But they are incomplete regarding what Paul says: 'I gave you milk, not food; for you were not able, and even now you are not able' (1 Cor 3:2). It is therefore foretold to her that she will bear a son, saying, 'You will call his name Ishmael' (Gen 16:12). This one will be a rustic man. In many ways, one who is not such is separated from the diligent, the wise, and the civilized. We say, therefore, as toward a citizen, and toward an expert, and toward an unlearned person, and toward a recently learned person, and toward a rustic.

Scripture. before: It was said previously regarding certain cages, machines, and hooks for men. These things happen such that even the most fearsome, like the lion and the leopard, whose nature is most wild, are often subjected to the hand of man. And thus the rule over them exists, God having provided this to them.

But it is necessary to know that the manner of rule exists in different ways. One rule is a legal supervision of both the ruler and the ruled; for the law gives authority and rule to the ruler and to the subject, so that in the same way the ruler rules and the subject is subjected, the law directing that it should be done thus. Otherwise, a teacher rules over students, and differently, a master over slaves, and a general over an army. Thus, man rules over irrational animals in different ways, as has been said: in some ways as domestic, in others according to their wild nature; for not all are edible, but some are already for medicinal use and for another contributing need, which the physiologist will find.

Furthermore, to these belongs the [word]: 'And God said, Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant spreading seed, which is upon the face of all the earth' (Gen 1:29). For God gave authority and knowledge, so that man might know which of those upon the earth is useful for food, and which for medicine, and which for another need. But there is a different nature to these: some are trees, some are vegetables, and some are grasses, and above all, some are edible and some are good for another use.

The need of these should not be ignored according to the command before this—when God said, 'Let the earth sprout herb-bearing seed-bearing plant according to its kind' (Gen 1:11), He adds, 'and a fruitful tree producing fruit' (Gen 1:12), because the trees differ from the herb, calling them 'fruitful trees'—not only does man exercise authority over those resulting from agriculture, but also over their materials which he neither sows nor cultivates, as he has different needs from these; for He does not make these things portable throughout the inhabited places, but it is evident that for the necessity of men, every plant has become a sprout; for all things are made for their use.

The providential character of God over all things is signaled by His declaration: "It shall be for food to you, and to all the beasts of the earth, and to all the fowls of the heaven" (Genesis 9:3). For it is fitting that He who cares for men should also provide for the animals that have become necessary and useful to them, and for other things useful to them; for indeed, not according to the prior logic of irrational things, but indeed through man, He has fashioned His providence. God saw all things again to be good, for they bring forth [fruit]: "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Before this, however, the word had praised each of the things coming into being by saying, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:25, 1:31) or "good"; but now it is stated with certainty, "very good," because of the harmony and concord of all things.

Let what is said be clear through an example. One who wishes to assemble a dance selects the best dancers for each part, so that nothing is lacking for their specific task; if, moreover, these are brought together for that which has prepared them, he will find the work resulting from their concord to be exceedingly and superlatively beautiful, which is not possible to result from a single person alone. One might also find this in a military camp: for it is necessary that there be a best spearman, a best archer, a best general, and a best counselor, so that when the time comes, the work of all being joined together may show the magnitude of praise, being referred to a single purpose. The word teaches that all things are "very good" (Genesis 1:31) by showing their interconnectedness, their proportion, their harmony, and their ordered state, and even the unshakable stability of opposites; which, as was said before, is not perceived by the senses, but is judged by the Word. before: Sometimes one perceives the evil that will come by an untimely desire for teaching; and if he does not desire it, he is nonetheless bettered by the habit of despising the divine, which comes to him through his own thoughts. For evil becomes long-lasting once the good has been despised, resulting in an unerasable state toward it.

The phrase 'unto the age' is placed instead of 'through life,' which is similar to what is said by Paul: 'I will not eat meat for an age, so that I may not scandalize my brother' (1 Cor 8:9, 23-24). And the Lord God sent him out from the paradise of luxury to work the earth from which he was taken, and He cast out Adam and settled him opposite the paradise of luxury.

If anyone asks how, since the serpent was the cause of the transgression and the woman was the first to be deceived, it is not said concerning them 'I was cast out,' but concerning Adam, who is said by the wise Paul not to have been deceived. We say that if he who suffered the lesser [sin] became [exiled] outside the paradise, how much more those who committed the great [sins]. For if the serpent was cast out, it is not yet clear whether the matter concerning the woman and Adam was worthy of being cast out from the paradise, since Adam, who is not subject to great errors, has become [exiled], it is clear that those who sinned greatly [are also subject to it].

It is also possible to presuppose concerning the woman that she was cast out together with Adam; for the name of Adam means 'man,' which the saying having this form confirms: 'And God formed the man male and female and called their name Adam' (Gen 3:20), which is 'He called their name man.' Concerning the serpent, it might be said that it was in paradise not as one worthy to pass time there, but just as it is said in Job that 'the angels of God came to stand before Him' (Job 1:6), so also it is said concerning the serpent.

Therefore, God sent out Adam—and it is clear that He also [sent out] the woman—from the paradise; and that which is being sent out has a time to return. For He did not send him out to have him in an irreversible state, but so that, having been settled, he might encounter...

He settled him lawfully, as was said before, putting into him the thought of the laws forbidding evil, which is an introduction to the good, not hiding paradise from him; for he did not take from him the knowledge of the good, nor did he make him forget the virtue in which he lived in paradise. Gen 3:24. And he stationed the cherubim and the flaming turning sword to guard the way of the tree of life. The names of the transcendent powers, as one might say, are not simply like the proper names among us, but significant of polities: principalities and authorities, thrones, dominions — from ruling and exercising authority and reigning (for this the throne signifies, according to what is said in Proverbs: “For with righteousness a throne of rule is prepared”), and dominions are so called from dominating. So the cherubim were called from what belongs to them: for “cherubim” is interpreted “multitude of knowledge.” From this very thing belonging to them the name was said. So too from Abram, Abraham was renamed, and from Sarai, Sarah, and from Jacob, Israel, and Peter […].

before: The animals entered the ark not in a confused mass, so that the ark would not be damaged by the sudden rushing of the waters through their joining together. The entry occurred in order, first Noah, through whom the others were saved, and then the others following him; thus the animals entered, which should be noted as having happened by divine power, for the numbering and bringing in was not by human endeavor, but had become a cooperation with God. Also, 'according to kind' is well-stated; for it was not possible for them to have the same sustenance, being divided by their natures. And he added 'in which is the spirit of life' for contrast with the dead. If anyone were to note how, then, the pure were not mentioned but the impure: 'two [two]' they say 'entered into the ark' (Gen 7:9), and it is clear that these were the impure; to which someone says that it is evident that, since the impure entered and the pure also entered, if the lesser entered, it is clear that the greater also entered. Furthermore, the 'two' could also be taken to refer to the pure, the word indicating that all entered in pairs.

And the Lord God closed the ark from the outside, and the deluge happened for forty days and forty nights upon the earth, and the water multiplied and lifted up the ark, and it was raised from the earth, and the water prevailed and multiplied greatly upon the earth, and the ark was carried upon the water (Gen 7:17-20). And following this history, the ark is closed 'from the outside' by the power of God, with no man being outside. And 'lifted up the ark' is also well-stated, uniformly and not suddenly, just as we previously set forth the reason.
