Even while the fraternal disposition and the extreme proximity for union are sufficient in the law, it does not permit these to be joined by marriage, but allows others with sisters and near relatives, so that through them they may be gathered together and from others [text gapped] and a disposition, which Cain suffered. For one must see even his hypocrisy in saying with thoughtlessness: 'I do not know; am I a guardian of my brother?' (Gen 4:9). For through the 'I do not know' the audacity is shown, because he thought he could hide from God; and through the 'Am I a guardian?' the unprincipled, irrational, and therefore senseless thing is revealed; for he ought to have been a guardian of his brother. And God said: 'What have you done? The voice of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth' (Gen 4:10). And now you are cursed from the earth, which had the stomach of its earth to receive the blood of your brother from your hand, because you work the earth and it will not add its strength to give to you; you shall groan and tremble upon the earth (Gen 4:11-12).

And the Philanthropist teaches while he is shameless, and thinking he can hide from God, he instructs him as this is impossible: 'The voice' he says, 'of your brother's blood cries to me from the earth' (Gen 4:10), do not suppose that the sleepless eye of Providence has escaped the stain. But he reveals it as a voice of blood, just as also elsewhere: 'Behold, the wages of the laborers who laid hold on your fields, who deprived you, cry out' (Jas 5:4). And so it is to be struck, and it is also possible that the blood is said to be there instead of the soul. And if anyone says that he was reminded because of this blood, that the body hid it; he also remembers the pouring out and how the earth had the stomach of its earth to receive the blood of a brother continuously, so that, growing large, the thing done might cause the hot-tempered one to be struck with remorse. And he brings upon him also curses, fittingly for one who worked so much, I say: 'And now you are cursed from the earth, because you work the earth and it will not add its strength to give to you' (Gen 4:12). For often, because of the sin of men, the poverty of the earth happens, not yielding its fruits according to what was said: 'The earth shall mourn because of those who dwell...'

In it. For it has been given to her to bear fruits to those who maintain a right calculation, and to those falling, providing the necessary things through the philanthropy of God; and again, by His command, those fruits which are lacking from her are restored, so that a return may occur. It is for a leading back; if we follow the first principles, God blames the hypocrite because he perverts the life-giving power of the soul, making it like the man outside, as it has been said. Therefore, he will be accursed, no longer providing fruits, but wasting his opportunity on something useless, so that from this he may be cast down into the beginning of virtue. For it is useful even to be perverted by evil, when the results from it are not attained, so that having undergone toil, he may be imbued with the love of virtue according to what was said: 'Egypt has toiled, and the commerce of the Ethiopians and the Sabaeans, tall men, shall pass over you' (Ezekiel 30:16). And 'groaning' and 'trembling upon the earth' (Psalm 55:6) shall be, thus being judged, always being reproved by the conscience.

And Cain said to the Lord God: 'My guilt is too great to be forgiven; if you cast me out today from the face of the earth and from your face I will be hidden, I will be a wanderer and a trembler upon the earth, and it shall be that everyone who finds me will kill me' (Genesis 4:9, 12, 14). The word of God remains even for those who are strangers to themselves, through which they take Him to be a philanthropist and good regarding His own; and it is not possible to cut away this good concept, even if they are often dissatisfied through the depth of wickedness. Immediately, therefore, those who are altogether forgetful of God, being surrounded by necessity, flee to supplications and entreaties, as is seen also regarding Cain. For as [God] was moved to pity regarding the murder of the brother and, after acting with boldness, hypocritically asking him, 'Where is Abel your brother?' (Genesis 4:9), yet, lest more perversion exist in man, having known from the words of God—through which he learned from the reproof of what had happened in his conscience—that the eye of God is unavoidable, he must not turn this [eye] toward all foreign things, from which it will happen to groan and tremble and to expect refutation from everyone who finds him.

before: Knowing not what day or what hour, he recalls a complete number, both days and accordingly. Just as 'God saw' (Gen 1:4) meant that it was good, so 'God saw' means as it is understood in the fading. We say these things to clarify the word, but these things could be for an ascent.

It was said before that 'let there be light' (Gen 1:3) must be raised to the Savior, not as emerging from non-existence, but as becoming fitting for those being enlightened. Among those being enlightened, some receive a lesser illumination and others a greater; and from these come those who experience a nocturnal state. Thus there are now luminaries of the Son's perception, following the will of the present matter: it fits each person's measure, becoming a sun of righteousness for those being raised, and for the lesser, being proportioned and providing a Spirit-illumination analogous to the moon.

And there were also those being enlightened in the night who, being perfect, necessarily provided for the body's need. For the perfect one, even if he is so, all at once, because he has a body, is nourished and undergoes the other needs of the body, which he himself makes perfect as a perfect one; for this reason he also has light, and such a light is a nocturnal light, since the intensity is so much relative to the body's needs, even if it is not lost, but experiences relaxation. And just as the moon itself receives rays from the sun and becomes a second light provided by the greater, so also the church is the light of the world.

For the Lord said to his own disciples, 'You are the light of the world' (Matt 5:14), not solar—for he himself was the sun of righteousness—but lesser and provided by him. But also the apostle, saying, 'In which you are as luminaries in the world' (Phil 2:15), shows that having participated in the true light, they are the light of the world; for he leads on: 'holding the word of life' (Philippians 2:16). And the relationship to this light of his might be a moon; for he did not say 'you are the lights,' but the light; for all having unity toward themselves, they are thus one light, being the church. And the stars of these would be subject to the Word, having ascended far above the others according to the allegory, whom...

And they shine. Those who were prophets, sending forth the dawn of the pre-proclamation before the rising of the sun. For He, having risen, guided the whole, and showed all things as one light, because those participating are shown to be perfect light.

For it has been said that the righteous will shine 'as the sun in the kingdom of their own Father' (Malachi 4:2), not 'sun,' but as the sun, just as it is also said in the Song concerning her sharing in the light: 'Who is this that rises like the dawn, beautiful as the moon, dazzling as the sun?' (Song of Solomon 6:10). And observe that some progress are revealed through these: first, one becomes like the dawn, then like the chosen moon instead of the full and uninterrupted [moon] according to the new moon—for even it is the same, being divided and not moon-like and oscillating, but its perfect state is according to the new moon, which he likens to the bride—and after which, although it is like the sun, it is a dazzling [wonder] because of much progress and union.

Those becoming such are not light by construction of this kind, but by participation in the true light. They also divide 'in the midst of the day' and 'in the midst of the darkness,' dividing evil from virtue, and thus illuminating those upon the earth, who are not yet heavenly through works. They also signify seasons and days and months and years, knowing the measure of each and how this one stands regarding instruction, just as we say of a physician that it is a time of nourishment based on how the one being fed stands, for even the one using medical art feeds at night.

Therefore, the sun of righteousness and the moon spoken of with it and the stars signify such a time as a time of lessons, a time of progress, a time of introduction; and they signify even the things themselves—for when someone is enlightened, the underlying things themselves are clear—not then under the sun of righteousness when it signifies, but being eternally [present], signifying when those advancing need guidance. Therefore they are also said to have come on the fourth day, signifying through allegory the relation toward logical matters. For as it was previously stated, being in potentiality of virtue, we need those who lead into the energy of virtues, which [comes] from...

For he who does the works of it is his child. And also well [is] 'from river to river'; for the virtue which is the due promise to the seed is that which is in the middle of flowing things, not being parts of the flowing things, but their boundaries; for if any virtue should become external to it, these things immediately encounter it. And if this has been said to the virtuous one because of the lying in wait of trials, you will understand, it being in the middle of those distressing [things] and overcoming them.

But Sarah the wife of Abram did not bear him children. And she had an Egyptian handmaid, whose name was Hagar. And Sarah said to Abram: 'Behold, the Lord has closed my womb; go in therefore to my maid, so that I may make children from her.' And Abram obeyed the voice of Sarah. The apostle led these to the two covenants by the law of allegory; and since the literal has also come to pass, it is also worthy to be seen. The holy ones lived together thus, not to hunt pleasures but for the sake of children. For such a tradition is brought about concerning them, that they only had intercourse with women when they had a time of conception; neither while nursing nor while feeding the infant, nor while pregnant, did they have intercourse; for in none of these times did they consider union to be appropriate.

And Jacob also confirms the tradition; for having tested in much time that Rachel did not accept to bear children, he no longer approached her; and she, thinking that if he approached her, she would bear, was saying: 'Give me children, or if not, kill me.' For he did not know that Jacob was not a potter, but was seeking union as if the holy one had ceased for the said reason, so that he might not labor in vain. And he said to her: 'Am I instead God to you, who has deprived you of the fruit of the womb?' (Genesis 29:31). And Sarah, being wise and holy, knowing for much time that through intercourse she had not received according to the belly, abstained from the fellowship with him, and since she knew that he would have children following [him], she gave her handmaid to him as a wife concubine. The temperance and also the abundance of Sarah and of Abram are shown.
The lack of passion comes not from one's own impulse, but through offspring produced by a woman. The explicit teaching is indeed useful, as we have explained.

The logic of ascent is smoothed out by using the pattern of the blessed Paul, who led the two women toward the two covenants; using this method in other matters, he led Sarah toward perfect virtue and philosophy, she being a married woman, free and noble, and living according to the laws; and virtue lives with the wise according to the laws, so that she may bring forth divine offspring from herself. For 'Wisdom' 'bears prudence to a man' (Prov 31:10), and it is said toward the pious and holy: 'Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine, your children like olive shoots around your table' (Ps 128:3). Thus the man who fears the Lord shall be blessed toward perfect virtue.

Sarah is led toward the spiritual, while Hagar the handmaid, the Egypt, is signified by Philo as the preliminary exercises and by Paul as the shadow. For it is impossible to grasp any of the spiritual or high notions without the shadow according to the letter or the introductory training; for one must first produce offspring from the lesser things. According to the shadow, they were immersing themselves, performing Pascha sensuously and circumcising themselves physically, being led by these things toward 'offering a sacrifice of praise to God' (Heb 13:15), which is the property of the free.

Since it is a matter of diligence for the wise to make room for the greater things, virtue proposes to use the introductory things first with a divine aim and to bring forth offspring from them. For since he who is now approaching virtue is not able to grasp perfection and thus bring forth from it, it is assumed that he first clothes himself in the preliminary trainings, so that he may also make room for it perfectly, if he is able.

As previously stated, Sarah offers the most precise example of temperance, having abundantly presented her own handmaid to Abram, observing that after...

before: Since therefore many men, having been born, were full of weakness, he says, 'My Spirit shall not abide in them.' For 'a holy spirit of discipline will flee from guile' (Ps 51:13); but guile is a more grievous passion, for it harms thoughtlessly. And 'unto the age' (Gen 6:3) signifies how such they are throughout their life. This is equivalent to 'I will not eat meat unto the age' (Ex 11:5). Whether therefore men are being driven by demons having taken daughters, or, as is previously rendered, the angels of desirable sensations, the Spirit does not remain in these. For whoever has come to this through passions and sins, it is evident that they have no part of the divine Spirit; for even those who have come for the help of the divine Spirit are deprived.

If anyone should be surprised at the saying that angels are souls, he ought not to marvel; for the spiritual is the same for both, even if an angel has a subtle body and the man a thick one; for to please God is common to both, since it is also common to the rational nature. And if anyone brings an objection as to how the pre-existing souls desired bodies, of which they did not know, it must be said to whom that desiring is often said not strictly as desiring that toward which their actions lead. Often indeed, also rebuking those living not well, saying, 'you desire to perish' (Matt 27:5), we do not say that 'you desire this very thing' (Acts 22:4), but 'you do such things which lead you to destruction' (Gal 6:7). If therefore anyone says that the souls desired bodies, it must be understood thus: that they were in such a state that they had need of the intercourse in the body, their being unworthy to be in a place not like this, after such actions.

Yes, 'and their days shall be a hundred and twenty years' (Genesis 6:3). Everything that God does and says, He does and says by a true judgment. Since therefore 'their days shall be a hundred and twenty' is said as a necessity, but this does not appear [to be so], it is necessary to interpret the intention of the thing foretold differently. The numbers received in the Scriptures were not received haphazardly, but for the sake of a certain word; often they are not even introduced naturally to the history, being received for the sake of a certain word. For to say, 'I left with myself seven thousand men, who did not do...' (1 Kings 19:18).

Because the history of bowing the knee to Baal is not possessed—for the holy one did not know so much—he was troubled for the sake of showing the thought, that everyone who surpasses the sensible and the world having been made in six days, having been brought forth in the restorative seventh week, is left by God as a goal for others and a benefit.

Thus also the number six was taken in the generation of this world as perfect, just as it has been said in the passages. And 'six times he is delivered from necessities' is not said because of the number or because of being delivered from necessities so many times, but rather, as long as one is in the things of the one having been made in six, he is under necessities, thus it is said; of the cessation, which is shown through the seventh, they do not have purification, as it was said to the disciples by the Savior: 'You are not of this world' (John 15:19) having surpassed the necessities in it.

These things were prepared beforehand to show that the number one hundred twenty is not in vain taken here; and it is necessary also to note this, that the scripture, taking the numbers, connects them with their own properties as of the world having been made in six days (Genesis 1). Let us take an example. For it is not possible to say that God made the world in six angels or in six monads or in six men; for time was being shown. Therefore, being offered in six days, it is said because time falls to the generation, being appropriately synchronized with the day, so as not to be years or months or hours; for the former is worthy of God, but the latter is the name of the incomplete; for not knowing what a day is, we are ignorant of the hour. And there, since it was concerning life, he mentioned years.

And... the many will say that God, as cutting off their life, established it at one hundred twenty, with the former living many years; but this was not fitting; for they seem to have lived more years. Let us therefore see the characteristic of the number. It is said therefore that this number, having been composed of its own parts, is doubled; for if the half is composed, which is sixty, the third is [missing], the fourth is [missing], the fifth is twenty-four, the sixth is twenty, the eighth is eighty-five, the tenth is [missing], the twelfth is [missing], the fifteenth is eight, the twentieth is [missing], the twenty-fourth is five, the thirtieth is four...

Often indeed, also rebuking those living not well, saying, 'you desire to perish' (Matt 27:5), we do not say that 'you desire this very thing' (Acts 22:4), but 'you do such things which lead you to destruction' (Gal 6:7). If therefore anyone says that the souls desired bodies, it must be understood thus: that they were in such a state that they had need of the intercourse in the body, their being unworthy to be in a place not like this, after such actions.

Yes, 'and their days shall be a hundred and twenty years' (Genesis 6:3). Everything that God does and says, He does and says by a true judgment. Since therefore 'their days shall be a hundred and twenty' is said as a necessity, but this does not appear [to be so], it is necessary to interpret the intention of the thing foretold differently. The numbers received in the Scriptures were not received haphazardly, but for the sake of a certain word; often they are not even introduced naturally to the history, being received for the sake of a certain word. For to say, 'I left with myself seven thousand men, who did not do...' (1 Kings 19:18).

Because the history of bowing the knee to Baal is not possessed—for the holy one did not know so much—he was troubled for the sake of showing the thought, that everyone who surpasses the sensible and the world having been made in six days, having been brought forth in the restorative seventh week, is left by God as a goal for others and a benefit.

Thus also the number six was taken in the generation of this world as perfect, just as it has been said in the passages. And 'six times he is delivered from necessities' is not said because of the number or because of being delivered from necessities so many times, but rather, as long as one is in the things of the one having been made in six, he is under necessities, thus it is said; of the cessation, which is shown through the seventh, they do not have purification, as it was said to the disciples by the Savior: 'You are not of this world' (John 15:19) having surpassed the necessities in it.

These things were prepared beforehand to show that the number one hundred twenty is not in vain taken here; and it is necessary also to note this, that the scripture, taking the numbers, connects them with their own properties as of the world having been made in six days (Genesis 1). Let us take an example. For it is not possible to say that God made the world in six angels or in six monads or in six men; for time was being shown. Therefore, being offered in six days, it is said because time falls to the generation, being appropriately synchronized with the day, so as not to be years or months or hours; for the former is worthy of God, but the latter is the name of the incomplete; for not knowing what a day is, we are ignorant of the hour. And there, since it was concerning life, he mentioned years.

And... the many will say that God, as cutting off their life, established it at one hundred twenty, with the former living many years; but this was not fitting; for they seem to have lived more years. Let us therefore see the characteristic of the number. It is said therefore that this number, having been composed of its own parts, is doubled; for if the half is composed, which is sixty, the third is [missing], the fourth is [missing], the fifth is twenty-four, the sixth is twenty, the eighth is eighty-five, the tenth is [missing], the twelfth is [missing], the fifteenth is eight, the twentieth is [missing], the twenty-fourth is five, the thirtieth is four...

before: For something to be destroyed is held back until the bad planting. And God saw that it was good. The land, therefore, having been hidden under the waters, was not dry and was not such as to feed animals or bear fruits.

And even after the establishment of the world and the being of animals, from which the successions come, to this it is good to be plants and trees and delicious fruits, from which the animals took sustenance. Since, therefore, as also previously was said, God seeing the analogy accepted and approved it, for this reason it is said: 'God saw that it was good' (Gen 1:10), the seeing being understood in the words to follow as meaning that not [the...]. Just as the craftsmen see the artificial things, and much more the God sees by a superabundance, He does not perceive [sensually].

And God said: 'Let the earth bring forth grass.' The underlying earth, having separated itself from the moisture, was named dry, being called land, and it has power to bear fruit. It must be observed that throughout the whole cosmopoeia what God said is intended and God made it, which shows the creative [power]; for especially through this precedence the creative is shown, but the name Lord shows the meaning of ruler and king. And 'In the beginning' (Gen 1:1) therefore 'God made' (Gen 1:1) is said, not the King or Lord, not that He is another, but that the name God presents the creative more emphatically. When therefore a command is given to Adam, it is said: 'The Lord God commanded Adam' (Gen 2:16), and rightly; for it is the work of a lord and king to give laws and commands.

And God therefore said: 'Let the earth bring forth grass, bearing seed according to its kind and according to likeness.' For of those growing from the earth, some are trees and some are vegetable plants. And Moses, wishing to call the trees in Deuteronomy, says simply 'the woody ones' [for] trees, the wooden ones, saying the vine, the fig, the olive, but it is evident also as many herbs [as] to the many people...

Regarding the medical treatments of bodies, Solomon shows that he has received from God the useful knowledge of these things, saying: 'For He himself gave to me the knowledge of what exists, to know the constitution of the world and the operation of the elements' (Job 28:23) and, with a little 'difference of plants and the powers of roots' and the nearby things, not yet calling them wood, but there he calls the herb or grass all things leafy, which also is called field-grass, just as in the Gospel it is called a plant in general, showing it through the similarity of the species.

For since even the Scripture knows the meaning of the species, it says: 'Abstain from every kind of evil' (2 Cor 7:1), using the word species specifically, and often instead of form it says: 'And we saw him, and he had neither species nor beauty' (Isa 53:2), and: 'For we walk by faith, not by sight' (2 Cor 5:7), meaning that the one who does not know through form walks by faith, but the one [who walks] by sight. Having spoken thus about the weeds or wild plants, 'sowing seed according to its kind' (Gen 1:11), he proceeds to the trees, 'wood that produces fruit' (Gen 1:11); for in every plant is the nature of its seed, whether they are edible, or for some other use, being known to men, or known only to God.

For he did not plow so that thorns might be reaped; this is not having farmed them well, nor [to] miss the blessing which Jacob blessed his son saying:

before: Ten years have not passed, and the impassibility of the wise man is because he aims to prepare [the soul] as it is suitable for the marriage. The matters of the upbringing have already been spoken of, that according to the aim of virtue, it is necessary to have first used the introductory things, so that through them he might first become a parent; and the children from the preliminary training are no less children of virtue because of the aim having done the same toward it. Having used this, therefore, he accomplished a better acquisition; for progress is most ready for the wise man.

"And he saw that she had conceived in the womb, and the lady was dishonored in her presence" (Gen 18:13). The aim, as has been spoken, is for the wise man to be trained in the preliminary training and in the shadow, so that having been trained in these things, he may proceed to the greater things; for as such a sequence is proper, so there is not a following return from the knowledge of the perfects into the smaller things. For the apostle neglects, writing to the Galatians, those who wish to live with the shadow of the law after the gospel (Gal 4:25). For the Jews, having the shadow as a companion, [are one thing], and the Galatians, after believing the gospel, wished to Judaize (Acts 15:5), having been deceived by a certain Ebion, who wished to Judaize after Christianizing and was persuading the others thus, since he had the epithet of this name among the apostles because of his making poverty manifest; for Ebion is interpreted as poor, because of his shallow and poor intellect, being called Ebion the poor; for that the Galatians were Greeks, Paul writes: "But at that time you did not know God, but served those which are by nature not gods; but now having known God, or rather having been known by God" (Gal 4:8). He therefore blames them, as has been said; for it is necessary to repay the promise of the Scriptures: "Having begun in the Spirit, are you now being perfected in the flesh?" (Gal 3:3); for having once been cast into a divine beginning, they were not appropriately seeking the types, for they were seeking them at an unseasonable time. For it is necessary to understand for what reason the sensory circumcision is given and until when...

For what period must he live as a citizen? If someone perceives this, he has fathered a child from a concubine, and after this he is able to perceive the circumcision being made in the heart by the Spirit (Rom 2:29). And this holy man, following the guidance of virtue, entered toward her to whom a maidservant had been handed to him, as we have shown, who also conceived, toward whom it is not fitting to remain thereafter exceeding what is necessary.

For many, having used preliminary exercises for the sake of complete instruction, having left behind them such things, are born in a slave-like manner and in a certain way dishonor virtue. But these things must not be referred to the person of Abraham, but to such a manner of those using this kind of way. And if, since we said that virtue... is the thing presupposing the things of the introduction, someone says that the offspring are a kind of part of it and such a person dwells with virtue primarily—for the underlying subject acts according to its postulates—it must be said therefore that of those things happening in time, some are prior to some and others are later, but when they are simultaneous, we take as understood that of those existing at once, one precedes and the other follows, as if regarding natural causes; virtue indeed is the cause of all things happening through it; therefore, even if such things precede it in time, it is by nature prior, just as marriage exists prior to child-rearing; for because of these things marriage... of virtue. And regarding the other sciences, the same...

Therefore, he who prefers other things to virtue dishonors virtue; for if someone were to choose it not for its own sake but for the sake of some other praise or glory, he in a certain way dishonors the good, it not receiving dishonor in itself. And take note that it has not even been said that Abram dishonored it—for this would not be harmonious with him—but since it is possible [to happen] from...

before: They have become like an ocean; this [element] has been gathered into one, and the others, as we say, have been gathered into parts. And 'and so the dry land appeared', and observe that it does not say 'all the dry land'. For under the waters there is land; for it is impossible to sustain water without having land or a corresponding body underlying it. But pay attention if there is a difference between saying 'dry land' and 'land' from what was said in the prophet: 'Once again I will shake the heaven and the earth, the sea and the dry land' (Isa 66:15).

Another says that the same thing is being indicated; yet by another thought, 'dry' and 'land' are named, as regarding the land as that which lies under the heaven, but regarding the dry element as being called so. For it is said, 'This is the sea of God and he himself made it, and his hands formed the dry land' (Ps 95:5), and concerning Jonah being cast from the belly of the sea-monster that 'the sea-monster approached and cast Jonah out onto the dry land' (Jon 2:10) from the liquid substance. These things indeed regarding the literal sense, but regarding the thought which follows the patterns, we say that the waters remaining above the firmament are not perceptible, nor are they part of these perceptible waters; for neither plants nor animals subject to this need of water find themselves there, and whatever was said before as indicative of nothing being water there is stated sufficiently as perceptible water.

We say, therefore, that what remains at hand will establish by its own logic that these are waters held in various and diverse collections under the firmament. For it is impossible for those in a state of discord to ever be of one mind; for discord is alien to both confusion and unity. For virtue is unifying, having a certain continuity. For indeed the temperate man is brave and wise and just, and he who has one [virtue] has the others, just as in the beatitudes in the Gospel (Matt 5); for he who has the one making-virtue has the others. And there often occurs a deviation regarding the same virtue, such as one being called merciful from the excess, and the just and other temperate man, and thus they are able to be [different] virtues. He who perfectly has one has the others, and I say 'perfectly' because of the frequent introduction...

That the virtues follow one another will be clear from this. The rational animal, set before itself to live according to virtue, uses prudence to judge what is to be done and not done, what is to be chosen and avoided, what brings blame and praise, since we have utter need of a science discriminating good and evil, that we may choose the one and flee the other. The one so disposed, having prudence and having divided the evil from the good, knowing altogether that the good is to be chosen and done, chooses it; and flees the opposite, knowing that it is both to be avoided and harmful and […] and damaging. And such a one needs justice too, so that he may assign to each what is fitting — to the good what is to be chosen, to the evil what is to be avoided. Having learned which things are blameworthy and which praiseworthy, he needs courage, that he may become despising of wiles, not being subject to the heretics. Hence such a one is also temperate; for temperance is fitting to the rational animal. And you see that the one who has one has them all, and these have one end as in the case of the beatitudes, though they are diverse.

For as, in a city where the entrances are diverse, the one entering through one is yet in the city, so also with the virtues. Unifying, then, is virtue, as Paul also says to those so living: “that you may be perfected in the same mind and the same judgment” (1 Cor 1:10). But vice is not so: for excesses cannot agree with deficiencies. For the one who has rashness does not have cowardice. Again, piety lies in the middle between impiety and superstition: piety is what accepts and reveres what must be, superstition is revering everything even what is not venerable, impiety is in no way revering anything nor holding anything sacred, which is the mark of atheists. Superstition and impiety could not run together, then. Since, then, the rational things under the firmament were held in vice and in inclination toward evil, and vice is disordered and confused, it is not possible for all to be in one mind or purpose. For as those voting, when they speak truth, bring forth the things of truth in one vote, while those who err either toward the less or toward the more, […] differently even in these, so also in the case of the […].

before: In the generation of the righteous, so that we might take the righteous with him, he himself was found righteous against [the world], not being entirely righteous against God being righteous; for only sons and women were found righteous against Noah. But it is great thus to be the opposite of God to be called righteous, as it is said: 'And the stars are not pure before him' (Job 9:21) and the other lights; but also in the psalms it is said: 'No living thing shall be justified before you' (Psalm 5:4), and again another saying he says: 'All our righteousness was as a garment laid aside' (Isaiah 64:6) from the presence of all the righteous.

From the clean animals he brought into the ark seven male and female, and from the animals not being clean two two male and female, and from the birds of the heaven the clean seven seven male and female, and from the birds not being clean two male and female, to breed seed upon all the earth. Consequently, 'seven seven' (Genesis 7:2) he commands to be brought in from the clean. Since they were for food and for religious services for men, and they themselves who remained in the ark had need, therefore more are taken, so that from them and a greater generation might arise a succession suitable for their needs; but concerning the others, having brought in this many, he commanded 'two' (Genesis 7:2) to be brought in.

And if it is necessary also to bring in natural philosophy by the word, one might say, as before, that since the two are divided, and this is characteristic of matter, the number two is characteristic of the unclean. But also, the two being taken away, the Savior calls 'into one new man' (Ephesians 2:15) the two, both the one from circumcision and the one from the Gentiles, bringing them into the unity of the commonwealth according to the Gospel, which the ancient saints had, there being no difference between Hellenism and Judaism. For from the arts of which there are statues, and with them idolatry, and after them the law, Judaism comes to be. The first of the human commonwealths, which was Christianity, though it did not have this name, according to the common...

A common notion exists, which even the Savior proclaimed: 'Whatever you want that men should do to you, do likewise to them' (Matt 7:12). This lies in the common notion; for whatever one does not want to suffer, he ought not to do to his neighbor. Because of this, it lies in the common notion, so that the man being led by God may be without reproach.

Later, when the notion is perverted, the Scripture is given, not to fight against that, but to lead men into it; for it is said: 'The law was given for help' (Rom 7:12). So also the Gospel has been proclaimed in the whole world, so that no one might claim to be unreminded of common notions.

These things, then, are [treated] as regarding the literal [sense]; but it must also be said that clean animals are introduced seven times seven. For to say what follows the history, that because they are to be used by men both for sacred rites and for food, they must be more [numerous], and also because of the logic of numbers, since it is much remembered in the Scripture: I say, in the seventh [day], God ceased (Gen 2:2)... many.

For regarding the unbegotten, those around the week [refer to] the birth; for this is virgin and without a father and without a husband, so that the said thing may be such. All numbers within ten, being doubled or tripled, except the seven, beget and are begotten, such as one begetting two, and two the four, thus having been begotten by the one, and the four the eight having been begotten by the two; and the five the ten; but the six, whenever it begets, does not beget, and the seven is neither begotten by those who preceded it nor does it beget anyone by itself until ten; but also the two the six and the three the nine, being tripled, beget.

before: Once the eyes were opened, they knew that they were naked (Gen 2:25). For this happens to those being deceived. For after the activity of their wickedness is made manifest, they come to realize that they were stripped of virtue; this is granted again by the pitiless God, so that he who works wickedness might not remain entirely insensate and stay completely outside of virtue.

This is the deception of the devil: that he makes the things seen according to the true logic by the eye of the pure soul to be seen conversely, supposing the pleasant instead of the good, and showing the good as something harmful. Thus also eyes are opened which previously were usefully closed. For there is in the soul an eye which imposes itself upon the intelligible through itself, but there is that which follows from instruction by another, which the serpent having perverted, filled the things of deception, so that both sensation and the mind would undergo harm; for when sensation suffers perversion, then also the opinions of the mind become diverted.

It has been said concerning those who have used things contrary: 'Woe to those saying the evil is good and the good is evil' (1 Tim 5:22). Thus, pleasures were raised up as the cause of errors; for even those in wisdom say they prefer the pleasant. For many prefer the easy way over virtue, not accepting the strenuous, and they are stripped because of it. Therefore, the pleasant things must be despised, since they become a hypothesis for sins.

There are some who say that 'Adam ate with it' (Gen 3:6) indicates his consent, so that he might not be utterly destroyed, agreeing with what was said by Paul: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14), as if he were able to turn away from the wickedness through her also. And they sewed fig leaves and made themselves girdles. And they heard the voice of the Lord walking in the garden, the cowardly ones, and both Adam and his wife fled from the face of God amidst the tree of the paradise (Gen 3:8). Remaining with the things previously viewed concerning the paradise and Adam and the woman, we connect these things. Since they knew that they were naked, having sewn fig leaves, they made themselves girdles; and having heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise at evening, they hid from the face of God in the midst of the tree of paradise. For it is fitting to say, not speaking ill of those following the history, how they sewed themselves girdles from fig leaves, and how those who had done things unworthy of it hear the voice of the Lord walking, and why he walks at evening, and further how they hid — what they thought concerning God — under the tree. For I think that in all these things they do not have a worthy saving of the sequence of the history, worthy of the narration from the Holy Spirit. We, then, as we have done in what went before, shall also in these perceive the divine element of what is written.

The word introduces two conditions of nakedness: one before the transgression, the other after it — the one shameless, the other known and producing shame. But it was also said in the things said before that, doing nothing worthy of shame but freed from every stain, they had their mind with boldness toward God — for such is virtue; but when they had become transgressors of God’s command, then stripped of the beauty of virtue, remaining naked of it, they were ashamed, reckoning from what goods into what evils they had fallen. Feeling still exposed, next they also hide from the God of all walking.

For the one sinning and not yet having cut out perception, but still cherishing the sin, is refuted by the common notions sown by God — the Maker ever crying out through them — but in still being held by the deception of the error, he often stitches together defenses of his sins. Or is this not clear in many? For often the one who has used anger procures plausible defenses, from which he will present the reasonableness of anger, sometimes even using the demonstration from the scriptures to establish his own will — which is the work of one stitching together from leaves and not from fruit some covering, not a perfect one; for this the girdle represents. For it is possible to hear the angry saying that even a saint in anger […].

before: Eighty-six and sixty-four, a cube, for four times four is sixty-four. But also, being tripled up to seven from the unit, the seven hundred twenty-nine is formed, and being both a square and a cube: one, three, nine, twenty-seven, eighty-one, two hundred forty-three, seven hundred twenty-nine, as it has been said, completes both a cube and a square; thus the square: seventy-two times twenty-seven is seven hundred twenty-nine; thus the cube: nine times ninety-nine is seven hundred twenty-nine. The square signifies stability, but the cube [signifies something else].

For if, even with such security made, the heretics find differences, introducing divinities, how much more would they find plausible arguments for their own evil hypothesis.

before: Having been struck, as if the protective power of God has departed from him, all other things are considered fearful by him, and he has no confidence in anything done by his own hand. These things are said to us regarding the whole scope of Cain's reply; but let us also see his mixed reply, which is faulty and does not partake of divine grace.

"Greater" he says, "is the cause for me to be forgiven," which would mean, according to a first understanding, that the evil upon me will be greater, if you, O God, do not pass over my injustice; for still, being under guardianship, the not-being-expelled is [a state]. This same thing is said regarding God in the prophet, concerning those of worthy consideration and those handed over to an unproven mind: "I will not visit their daughters when they play the harlot, nor their virgins when they commit adultery. For when they are sinning, those whom he wishes to train, he says: 'I will visit their lawlessness with a rod and their sins with whips, but my mercy I will not withdraw from them.'" (Ezekiel 16:25; Ezekiel 20:47).

What he says now, that is, that the reproach from you, Lord, will be greater than me, as previously stated; and since he thinks himself having stumbled and having suffered a perversion, he thinks that having been cast out from the earth, he will be cast out from the face of God. According to another understanding, he might be saying these things, that the evil to me will be greater if I remain in the land, O God, lest you destroy me into non-existence; for if you cast me out from the earth, and from your face I will be hidden, no longer existing, which was possible for him, but since you do not cast me out from the earth—for this must be obeyed—I shall be in it groaning and trembling, from everyone finding me and killing me.

For many, when they know for themselves the immeasurableness of their errors, having some notion that God himself will visit them, they consider non-existence to be preferable, preferring to suffer insensibility to existing; this would be clear from what was said by the prophet concerning the traitors of Jesus: "They will wish it if they were consumed by fire." (2 Thessalonians 1:9). And in another way he might be imposing [this meaning] to his saying: "If you cast me out," and asking for a place of repentance today so that the present might be surpassed, "today"...
It was said. But he also desired that the one called 'his own' might fall into perfection toward God, so that he would not lie exposed to anyone finding him for destruction.

Cain might have wondered at any time, finding him and killing him, that nothing existed at all besides him and the mothers; to whom one might say that, having first the idea that a succession of men was to come, he feared that having worked such a great defilement, he might be destroyed as an abomination by those coming, the weight of which would pass upon the born ones as well; then, even if not this, he suspected that divine powers would be vengeful for the impious deed, which he was likely to have seen the pouring out of the evil.

But regarding the bringing back: And the Lord God said to him, 'Not thus' (Gen 4:15); everyone who kills Cain, seven avenges he will release. And the Lord God set a sign for Cain, not to kill him, everyone finding him. For a greater punishment, or according to the suspicion of Cain, that everyone finding him kills him, protecting the murderer of his own brother, God says, 'Not thus' (Gen 4:15); that is, this justice of the transgression is not suitable to you, to be destroyed by him. before: Thus the phrase 'and God made' is brought in. Immediately, for since according to the succession of living things, the successors in this generation cast the seed, but God forms and fashions it, this is to say, it happens to be the first command, and then the bringing forth of the seed is the perfection of God.

God says concerning man, according to Jeremiah: 'Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you' (Jeremiah 1:5). The diversity of the existence of living things is varied; some having their generation from the beginning out of earth and waters, while the succession occurs differently. For some are oviparous, from which the eggs will be, and others are viviparous, God's will having provided a diverse manner for the existence of these. before: Four hundred sixty-two, one hundred twenty-one, makes the total four hundred forty, being double the one hundred twenty, of which the parts are fifteen, just as fifteen increased by progression makes the one hundred twenty. That the fifteen was received into the most perfect degree is clear; for of that same number six degrees [are missing]. But also the 'giving a portion to the seven', which signifies the Old Testament, and 'also to the eight', which is a symbol of the Resurrection and the New Testament, joins the fifteen. For the Jews, receiving only the old, give a portion to the seven, not hearing that it also gives to the eight; but also the heretics, setting aside the old, giving a portion to the eight, refuse to have the seven provide; the ecclesiastical, receiving both covenants, gives a portion to both. Since therefore also the one hundred twenty number is doubled, there exists a symbol of teaching being awakened toward the true life according to both practice and contemplation, honored, so that having doubled the life, they may have this life, being made manifest through the number, in order that the said thing—that he who lives not also by practice and contemplation does not live, but just as the profligate has died—may be true.

4. And the giants were upon the earth in those days and after that, as the sons of God were approaching the daughters of men and they became to themselves (Gen 6:4). Those were the giants from of old, the men who are named. Those outside the faith, bringing this in from myths, bring it in; but in the Divine Scripture, instead of strong men, they are named. before: They present their offerings as thanksgiving, doing so naturally; but those who use them carelessly, as if keeping the precious things for themselves and offering the cheap ones, have made a poor choice. Since Israel does this very thing, the prophetic word says rebukingly and admonishingly: 'If you bring a blind man for sacrifice, is it not bad? And if you bring a lame or sick man, is it not bad? Bring him to your leader' (Malachi 1:8).

But also Ananias and Sapphira in the Acts of the Apostles, when many were offering for the needs of those in need, they themselves received the price of a field, from which, having decided upon it, they brought the half and the other half making a poor choice, which the apostle's spokesman, inspired by the Spirit, rebuking said: 'Was it not still yours, and was it not under your control when you sold it? Why did you dare to do this in your heart?' (Acts 5:3-4). This also was said to Cain by God: 'Why are you so troubled, and why is your face downcast? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned' (Genesis 4:6).

For all sin as they bring to God as a needy person, ignoring what was said in the Psalms toward Him, the God: 'Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?' (Psalm 50:9) and also: 'Mine are all the beasts of the field, cattle on the mountains and oxen' (Psalm 50:10). For all that you have in abundance from me, I also have all things, so that one not in need did not command, but rather from these, using them symbolically, it is fitting to use virtue not carelessly, but perfectly and completely.

Furthermore, in order that the evil may not advance, it is exhorted to be at rest from it, so that by rubbing against it one might not work up a worse sorrow. In this way it is also said to Zion, being moved disorderly—for such is the name—'Stand up, you, Zion' (Isaiah 62:1). Since the rational animal is active, either working out evil or virtue, in a manner of speaking,

When one does evil, it is appropriate for him to stand against this, so that virtue may find the space that is becoming. This indeed David advises: 'Turn away from evil' (Psalm 34:14), saying, 'and do good' (Psalm 34:14). 'Be still' (1 Kings 19:12), therefore, he says, do not progress through evil; do not consider through negligence as if your sacrifice was not properly received. For many, often stumbling themselves and for this reason not having God as a co-worker, are displeased with providence, which God prevents in Cain, saying: 'Be still' (1 Kings 19:12).

And also the 'his turning toward you and you shall turn him back' (Psalm 94:7) comes, teaching that whatever is offered to God not according to what is becoming, these things are not offered to him, but belong to the Giver, turning back toward him because of not having found a place in God. So also those providing alms for the sake of being seen by men withhold their own reward, having nothing from God; for they did not do this with a divine purpose. The whole discourse of the word is most useful for character, and thus being taken simply, it teaches sincerely regarding offerings and not to do them carelessly; and since we lead the aforementioned into the modes of the soul in the instances of errors, it is necessary even now to do this.

before: And the Lord said to Abram: 'Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house into the land which I will show you; and I will make you into a great nation, and I will bless you, and I will magnify your name, and you shall be blessed, and I will bless those blessing you, and those cursing you I will curse; and all the families of the earth shall be blessed in you' (Gen 12:1-3).

Not as a total exclusion does God command Abraham to depart from his land and his kindred, but seeing in him something worthy to be remaining arranged under his guardianship, which was the faith in him; for the one having faith in God was not bound to remain with the foolish, since his father was an idolater. For often the company of the evil harms the diligent, and especially when they are fresh. Because of this also the Savior preaches: 'If anyone wants to come after me and does not hate his father and his brothers and sisters and also his wife and children, he cannot be my disciple' (Luke 14:26).

It was not hatred of the kin being worked by this that the Lord said, but if something of these things became an obstacle toward virtue, it is to be hated for the sake of virtue, which the disciples, having done, said: 'Behold, we have left all and have followed you' (Matt 19:27).

This therefore also now is commanded to the patriarch, God promising to show him a land so that he may live there, to make him into a great nation, and to bless him and to magnify his name and to show him blessed, so that those blessing him find blessing from him, and those cursing him receive a curse from him. And in addition to these, it is promised to him that all the families of the earth shall be blessed in him, which are not all human, as we are entering from the lifting up, beginning from those above. For the devil is the father of every sinner according to the...

It has been said: 'Everyone who does sin is of the devil' (1 John 3:8). For just as he who does the will of God becomes his offspring—for he says, 'Everyone who does righteousness is born of God' (1 John 3:7)—so 'the one doing sin is of the devil' (1 John 3:8) and of his father. And there is also a kinship through the composition of this father.

Therefore, God exhorts him to explain this, calling it earth, for it is nothing heavenly but all earthly in the opposing devil, so that, casting off the image of the swine, he might take up the image of the heavenly. before: A seed, so that having nourished them they might send them far away, and also of the most beast-like men, concerning whom it has been said: 'Become not like the horse and the mule, to whom there is no understanding' (Psalm 32:9), and: 'You have become female horses.' But the holy ones begin all these things, having transferred them from the hands to better things through the Word. But man has also received authority over the creeping things, which, when he carries them toward pleasures and passions, he would not sin, by abstaining from fleshly desires in the overcoming of them and killing 'the members upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness, passion, desire, evil' (Colossians 3:5).

And rightly, according to the reciprocity, it is said: 'And God made the man, according to the image of God He made him' (Genesis 1:27). For the command containing, at the 'according to the image,' the making of him 'also according to likeness,' the text states that 'according to the image He made him,' without adding the 'according to likeness,' concerning which we discussed briefly before. And the 'male and female He made them' (Genesis 1:27) is to be examined: how, concerning one man commanded by God, the reciprocity says: 'He made them.' And this might be a demonstration according to the literal sense of the woman being consubstantial with the man, being categorized under one kind of them, and because of this the saying 'let us make man' (Genesis 1:26) was uttered; but the 'male and female' is a representation of the parts for the sake of the succession which God established, showing at once also that the woman is 'according to the image of God' (Genesis 1:27), both of them being recipients of the same, both of the imitation and of the participation in God and the taking up of virtue of the Holy Spirit.

And since we were saying that the approach of man is made manifest also in the intellect and soul, let us consider by anagogical ascent thus the 'male and female': just as the one, being able to be a capable teacher, as being able to receive the seed of the Word into the souls capable of receiving it, so if he were male,

They symbolically possess the place of the female, being unable to conceive anything of their own, but receiving instruction from others like the manner of sowing. In the sensible realm, the female and male are made by God; but in the intelligible realm, one possesses a place for himself through his own choice or a teacher, who is male and a sower of good things, or a disciple receiving the seed of another and thus becoming female.

Thus anyone might perceive the greater things through the lesser of the rational. If one wished to take it regarding the Word of God, every rational nature would have a female rank toward Him. This is a bridegroom of the rational essence; for 'he who has' is 'the bridegroom of the bride' (Song of Solomon 2:16). And in the Song of Songs, a bridal song is sung of a bride to a bridegroom, the church being understood as the bride, or the perfect soul already able to be joined to the Word, who is the sower of every rational essence, this essence receiving the benefit from Him both in moral and in the doctrines of truth.

Regarding the sensible, a change of nature is impossible; but regarding the intelligible, a man currently receiving lessons and therefore being in a female rank might at any time, through progress, become as others become a teacher, just as one might again, from sloth, fall away so that he is barely able to receive from another what he himself formerly instructed others. before: They act without being recognized. It is not necessary to suppose it is a lie that the time of every man has come, even if eight were saved in the ark; for here the general has been taken instead of 'for the most part'.

If, however, the 'every man' says, 'For where are strife and jealousy among you, are you not men?' (James 3:16), Noah is not subject to this by surpassing the human condition; and thus it is true that the time of every man has come, according to that which is called to sin in this way. Nor is 'against me' added in vain; for no mortal possesses the knowing of the time, by which one might have worthily acted so that the rest might have been made known. For this indeed no mortal truly knows; for if he were knowing the hearts, he would not even have helped by quickly turning back those who had come into sin.

For the only thing belonging to the unexceedable goodness, the goodness of essence which is not diminished, is to see the hidden and to know the time. If even someone of mortals participates in goodness from God by disposition, yet he is ignorant of the impositions of sins and the causes, just as God, knowing all, knows the time of the reprimand, therefore it is said 'against me' and 'because the earth was filled with injustice from them'. It is fitting that this too is said; for punishment does not come upon them because of the sins of others. It is also evident from this that such a death did not come upon them by fate; for since he says 'the earth was filled with injustice from them', the time has come, which would not have been established, unless they were sinning.

Yes, and behold, 'I will destroy them and the earth' (Genesis 6:13). The philanthropy and goodness of God are shown through these by foretelling what is to come, so that by the fear of what is expected, he might restrain the evil, which also happened to the Ninevites upon hearing the prophet Jonah: 'In three days Nineveh shall be overthrown' (Jonah 3:4). Consequently, too, to the righteous man he foretells these things and pre-arranges the making of the ark, putting forward this construction more clearly for the sake of every proclamation toward repentance, and he promises to destroy them and the earth, since it was necessary for this. For there are many reprimands given by God for the sake of the recognition of sins occurring; he wants...

For he says that he wished to gather all men into the knowledge of truth, as a bird gathers its young under its wings, but you did not wish to (Matt 23:37). For necessity does not force the good to become so, nor is it possible; for such a thing is no longer good. But when God, knowing all things, after many admonitions finds those whom he admonishes not obeying, he destroys them, according to what is profitable for his judgment. And the earth is also destroyed—that is, the things in the earth—for this is what 'the earth' signifies appropriately; for the things of men perishing, it was necessary for the things standing through them to pass away also. Just as the birds were left behind through Noah and those with him, and likewise the birds of all other animals were left behind.

You shall make the ark by gathering [pieces] together, and you shall complete it one cubit by one cubit upward; and you shall make the door of the ark on the side. Make for it two or three decks. The phrase 'of squared timber' has the greater following, being commanded to make Noah's ark, first so that much time would not be consumed in dividing them, and secondly, which is more truthful, so that being made from whole timbers it might be more secure; for it was going to encounter storms and not a small gale, against which it would not have withstood if it had not been constructed from whole timbers. And 'the sick' is also useful, which are divided places, because of these two things: first, so that the habitation of the animals, which he was going to bring with him, would not be mixed, and second, for the joining of the construction; [it is] weaker...

before: Has Adam become like one of us, knowing good and evil? And might he not ever stretch out his hand, take the fruit of the tree of life, eat, and live forever? Many take this word spoken to Adam mockingly, saying something unsuitable of God. For it is not fitting for a serious man to stumble over a trifle, much less God.

Since, they say, the serpent promised this to the woman, saying: 'For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:5), God said to Adam after he transgressed: 'Behold, Adam has become like us,' mocking him. Therefore, we, driving away such a notion from God in accordance with the will of the divinely inspired scripture, have taken up what is set forth.

The devil is not by nature evil or in essence, but he became good and well, having become devil, satan, and evil through a personal change; but then he was good and well when he held a place in the rank of angels, but he departed from them, cast down to earth because of the pride he conceived for himself. Thus he did not say to Adam: 'Behold, you have become like one of us,' but 'like one of us'; for from the heavenly ones this one fell, just as the psalmist teaches, saying: 'I said, you are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High, but you die like men and fall like one of the rulers' (Ps 82:6). For he too is a ruler and a god, not by essence, but by god-making, and he fell like those about whom it is said: 'I said, I begot sons and raised them, but they rejected me.'

'Behold, Adam has become like one of us,' he led on how? 'To know good and evil.' For only those not using virtue possess this, knowing only what is good and what is evil, without restraining themselves to choose the good and flee the evil. Instead, they use things in a shifting way, according to those who are debated about whom it is said: 'Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness' (Isa 5:20). And thus God says 'of us' to his own angels, just as...

He is a bodyguard to his own. But when it is known from the Scriptures that God makes himself common with his own creatures, it is learned from what was said to the disciples by the Savior: 'Rise up, let us go from here' (Matt 26:38), which also does not have a small significance in its observation; for indeed 'rise up' is toward them, but 'let us go' is with them.

Since the Savior 'did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth' (Rom 7:7), therefore he has not become [subject to it] by a fall, and such a rising is not necessary for him as it is for the disciples, to whom he said, 'Rise up,' 'Arise from the human things,' and he counts in his departure himself. Since human nature alone does not have the power to use virtue without the breath of God, because of this he says, 'Let us go from here'; for he himself is both shepherd and staff, which guides over divine things.

Indeed, he also said to the thief: 'Today you shall be with me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43). But it is also said in the unholy thought directed toward men in the Tower of Babel: 'Come, let us go down and let us pour out their tongue' (Gen 11:7). For even if he does what God wills through subordinate angels—but I say his judgment is happening in the things that occur—it is said that he descends with those sent by him.

'Behold,' he says, 'Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:22), to whom he goes as a condemnation, yet in a nurturing way, the Philanthropist. For he performs both the threats and the inductions toward the beneficial. And what is it that he says: 'And now, perhaps one day he will stretch out his hand and take of the tree of life and live forever' (Gen 3:22)? Envy has driven him away from the divine dance; if it were this, it would be impossible for him to exist much more and superabundantly in God.

Therefore, he does not prevent them from taking the Tree of Life again out of envy, but he prevents them unsuitably. For just as the Savior commands: 'Do not throw the holy things to the dogs, neither your pearls before the swine' (Matt 7:6), and he also brings forward the reasoning, saying: 'lest they trample them and turning, tear you to pieces' (Matt 7:6), so it is not good for one having become in sins and still being in them to receive the life of the tree; for such a thing is contemptible. If the worthless one were prevented from such a guidance, not...

Thus he did not say to Adam: 'Behold, you have become like one of us,' but 'like one of us'; for from the heavenly ones this one fell, just as the psalmist teaches, saying: 'I said, you are gods and all of you are sons of the Most High, but you die like men and fall like one of the rulers' (Ps 82:6). For he too is a ruler and a god, not by essence, but by god-making, and he fell like those about whom it is said: 'I said, I begot sons and raised them, but they rejected me.'

'Behold, Adam has become like one of us,' he led on how? 'To know good and evil.' For only those not using virtue possess this, knowing only what is good and what is evil, without restraining themselves to choose the good and flee the evil. Instead, they use things in a shifting way, according to those who are debated about whom it is said: 'Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness' (Isa 5:20). And thus God says 'of us' to his own angels, just as...

He is a bodyguard to his own. But when it is known from the Scriptures that God makes himself common with his own creatures, it is learned from what was said to the disciples by the Savior: 'Rise up, let us go from here' (John 14:31), which also does not have a small significance in its observation; for indeed 'rise up' is toward them, but 'let us go' is with them.

Since the Savior 'did no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth' (1 Peter 2:22), therefore he has not become [subject to it] by a fall, and such a rising is not necessary for him as it is for the disciples, to whom he said, 'Rise up,' 'Arise from the human things,' and he counts in his departure himself. Since human nature alone does not have the power to use virtue without the breath of God, because of this he says, 'Let us go from here'; for he himself is both shepherd and staff, which guides over divine things.

Indeed, he also said to the thief: 'Today you shall be with me in Paradise' (Luke 23:43). But it is also said in the unholy thought directed toward men in the Tower of Babel: 'Come, let us go down and let us pour out their tongue' (Gen 11:7). For even if he does what God wills through subordinate angels—but I say his judgment is happening in the things that occur—it is said that he descends with those sent by him.

'Behold,' he says, 'Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil' (Gen 3:22), to whom he goes as a condemnation, yet in a nurturing way, the Philanthropist. For he performs both the threats and the inductions toward the beneficial. And what is it that he says: 'And now, perhaps one day he will stretch out his hand and take of the tree of life and live forever' (Gen 3:22)? Envy has driven him away from the divine dance; if it were this, it would be impossible for him to exist much more and superabundantly in God.

Therefore, he does not prevent them from taking the Tree of Life again out of envy, but he prevents them unsuitably. For just as the Savior commands: 'Do not throw the holy things to the dogs, neither your pearls before the swine' (Matt 7:6), and he also brings forward the reasoning, saying: 'lest they trample them and turning, tear you to pieces' (Matt 7:6), so it is not good for one having become in sins and still being in them to receive the life of the tree; for such a thing is contemptible. If the worthless one were prevented from such a guidance, not...

before: He works the corruption of the earth. For this made men blameless, if the inability to be adorned toward God worked a sorrow; but the hardship of ways is shown through the corruption of the earth, just as it was foretold, of men corrupting the way of God, which had taken hold to prosper toward blessedness. Such are those having heard the words of Jesus and not doing them.

And if it also shows the flesh of man, as is often said, one should observe whether 'all flesh corrupted his way' (Genesis 6:12) shows how each man has strayed from his own opinion. But that flesh is said instead of man is clear from 'I will pour out from my spirit upon all flesh' (Joel 2:28), and 'He will judge all flesh' (Isa 40:6). Therefore all those of the generation of Noah, having become earthly and fleshy, each strayed from 'his way' (Gen 6:11) which he had received; for the way is called to be received of him and to be given to God. Thus they corrupted their own way or the way of God; for both are possible.

And God said to Noah: 'The time of every man comes against me, because the earth was filled with injustice from them' (Gen 6:11). Many of the written things have a more useful history for the many. For these, living by sensation and glory, do not reach the truly great and profitable things. And let the said thing be upon an example.

Jesus healed a blind man from birth, and Lazarus, having had four days in the tomb, he brought out by command alone, and again the one in the cave, remaining in much decay, he raised. These things were for the sensible fulfillment and were symbolic: the one [healing] the blind from birth showing the sight of a soul that had never seen, because it had been overturned in sin and ignorance from soft nails, and again the one already pathless and having lost hope, having fallen from the blessed life, was shown symbolically coming back to it through Jesus, and the one seized by decay, then having been saved, testified to the return of a soul falling into insensibility. But these are more wonderful and greater than the healing of bodies, since the essence of the soul is more precious than the body, but which the many do not know. He, therefore, explaining the paradoxes thus to them, makes it more useful, and in the things now set forth of the history...

It also has a more useful benefit for the many. For what does he say? 'The opportunity for every man has come upon the earth' (Luke 19:44). And Peter also says that by the patience of God the deluge was delayed, so that repentance might be given.

For it has been revealed that the construction of the ark took place in a hundred years, so that seeing men and inquiring about the cause might take the opportunity for repentance. But opportunity here must not be thought of as being called by someone a time-keeper; for not fate holds sway over things, but everything happens by the will of God.

Therefore, it should be understood that 'the opportunity for every man has come upon the earth' means the almost-fullness of the sinning men, by which the bringing on of vengeance must be approached, as it is said: 'For the iniquities of the Amorites are not yet full unto this time' (Gen 15:16), instead of saying 'they have not sinned so much that their repentance be known.' For God does not bring wrath upon every single day, even though sins are being committed; rather, He does this by providing a place for repentance and giving the opportunity to recognize their own sinning; but when thus the things concerning them are completed so that they no longer have opportunity to recognize [their sin], the time has come for them to suffer.

And once the mention of the filling up of sin has occurred, this is to be noted: that it is not the same to fill up sins in one man and in a whole nation. For among the many, all sins are found to be present, such as one being unmanageable and another being spared, one being bold and another cowardly, and again one being licentious and another being foolish; but for one man, it is impossible to find these opposing vices in excess and deficiency. For it is possible for all virtues to be in a man, for they follow one another, but the vices are not so, because of the things previously mentioned.

And these things being a digression, let us return to the beginning: 'The opportunity for every man has come.' No one has such sins that they might be forgiven him; and just as an excellent physician, even if it happens at night, sets a time for the sick to receive nourishment according to the state of the disease, so also is the present thing being said. For when men have reached the extremity of sin, through which the deluge is brought, this happens.

before: And the decorations of these, or of the doves, are adorned in the greenness of gold, the gold signifying the mind, and the greenness symbolizing life and incorruptibility.

Therefore, those who are adorned by wisdom—by which God wills that the creeping things to be removed from the waters (Gen 1:20)—these are doves having another mind, being raised up by the wings of truth and always having the life-giving Spirit within themselves. God likewise blesses these very things, so that they may receive multitude and increase; multitude so that they may imitate others, and increase so that they may always have love for the perfection of the good.

And the command 'and fill the waters' (Gen 1:22) would signify that you are no longer being submerged by the bonds of sin, but you continue to dwell, holding yourselves above yourselves. Or perhaps, since water has its own fullness and use for cleansing and watering, both to soak and to sustain, it advises that, turning away from those things which happen under it by intention or by aim—where I say being constricted and submerged by the chains of sins—you move toward those [activities]: the being watered from pure water and not being constricted, and being cleansed, being freed from all filth, fulfilling these activities of the water, being watered from the immortal water and being cleansed, but not being constricted.

And 'there was evening and there was morning, the fifth day' (Gen 1:23) signifies thus how the day of the sensible reaches its end upon the intelligible; for the end of the passing day becomes the beginning of the one that follows. Therefore, having left the sensible, they move toward the perfect, which is signified by the number six; for the progress of the five leads toward the six. Yet these things are not to be observed by number alone, but according to the meanings within the numbers: the five signifying the sensible, and the six signifying the perfection of the present.

And God said: 'Let the earth bring forth a living soul according to its kind, four-footed and creeping and beasts' (Gen 1:24). Likewise, what God said before must be observed; He said so that the earth might bring forth living souls, which serves as a demonstration...

The souls of irrational animals are not joined to their bodies as they are being corrupted, unlike the souls of humans; for these [irrational souls] remain even after dissolution. Many, including those outside the faith, agree to this, thinking it is a light matter, though they have only a dim conception of the whole; they say it is a fading thing, but that there is a certain place where souls rub themselves after their departure from there.

Indeed, the command regarding irrational animals is that the earth should bring forth a living soul according to kind—quadrupeds and creeping things and beasts—as the command subjects it; for the earth has the power of the irrational animals coming out of it, a kind of logos-seed existing in it, but rather in the seeds of the animals, this being closer, since the irrational souls provide the imaginative and impulsive motion to the bodies, being themselves corporeal, but rather being in the body and in its composition. For they say, 'The soul is the blood of every living thing' (Gen 2:7). The common things to them are feeding, watching, sleeping, and tiring. But the command is not about every soul, but only about irrational ones; for the human soul is created according to the image and likeness of God, as will be known more precisely in the following.

Furthermore, since the animals brought forth from the earth are not all alike but are submitted to different forms according to kind, he said 'according to kind' (Gen 1:24), signifying the form. Thus, kind is common to them; for all living things have departed [from non-living] by slight differences in essence; for the essence of a horse is different from that of an ox, and of others likewise. And the command is made for three [kinds]: quadrupeds and beasts and creeping things, not all quadrupeds and beasts being present. So perhaps one would call the quadrupeds that are useful to men today 'quadrupeds,' but the beasts are those quadrupeds that are countless, and the creeping things are whatever is serpent-like, and the differences of these are not unknown to those who have studied history. And it happened thus (Gen 1:24). For it was necessary that the reality should follow the command. And if anyone were to be surprised by the 'and it happened'...
