before: A person who is conscious of their own sin maintains boldness. Regarding what happens after correction, the Master of all says he shakes his understanding again: 'Who told you that you were naked, if not from the tree from which I commanded you alone not to eat, from it you ate?' (Gen 3:11). The word is philanthropic; for God again holds to the one who sinned, indicating the thought of the commandment. For it was necessary, after all things, to partake of both the known good and the evil, and not only.

For, as previously stated, the human [nature] entering in without the energy of virtue is most harmful, but with all things it is useful; which God also commanded like the manner of a good physician, providing a most useful drink for health, which when held together is effective, but when divided harms, just as it is previously stated regarding the so-called 'beast-like' [diet]. Such is what the Lord says he is teaching in the Gospels: 'Become wise as serpents and innocent as doves' (Matt 10:16).

But regarding these things, Adam says he blames the woman: 'The woman whom you gave with me, she gave to me from the tree and we ate' (Gen 3:12). Envy is a friend to malice, and it is the property of those who sin not to quickly confess the sin, but to divert the blame of the slip. For some think that men give their lives to fate from that [source] and are compelled toward sin, while others say that all things happen by chance and think that these things happen just so. But the first-formed [man], having heard the commandment, says: 'The woman whom you gave with me' (Gen 3:12).

It was necessary for him to understand that first, having received her from God, he also properly received her and that which is advantageous; then, he did not receive her as a teacher, but as one following him. And this we perceived in the fallen ones from the response of the Eve toward the serpent, speaking to him: 'We eat from the fruit of the tree of paradise, but from the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the paradise God said: Do not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die' (Gen 2:17); for God had not commanded concerning touching, but she, having learned this as if from Adam, was being taught to be more reverent, since, being weak, she heard from him not even to touch it. How then [can] the teacher and guide [be...] from the one being led into deception...

Those defending Adam argue from what was said to him: 'The woman whom you gave me with me' (Gen 3:12), for since he said she was given to him with him, knowing that she would be cast out due to disobedience, he accompanied her not to participate in transgression, but for her benefit; for often teachers sympathize with the weaker, so that through this they might work out a repentance for them.

And these things they hold from what is said by Paul, which leads to Christ and the Church: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14). It is understood, being referred to the woman's church and to Adam's Christ, to preserve the chain of allegory and to avoid the possibility that the human race, from which the church is fulfilled, might have used the transgression as a cause for the descent of the Savior, so that he might use the economy, through which curse and sin came, not being these things, but having received them through us.

And the Lord God said to the woman: 'What is this that you have done?' and the woman said: 'The serpent deceived me and I ate' (Gen 3:13). Three persons are introduced by blame here: the man, the woman, and the serpent. And the man had an apology that the woman had become a hindrance to him in eating from the forbidden tree, from which he knew he was naked; but the woman blames the serpent, saying: 'The serpent deceived me and I ate'; for God also sought the cause of the slip from them; but such a question is not borne toward the serpent. For he did not have the cause of the evil to lay upon another, being himself her progenitor.

This also the Lord teaches in the Gospels, saying concerning him: 'When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and his father is the father of lies' (John 8:44); that is, the father of lies; for the devil does not have a father according to those who act mythically. But all those using evil, except him, do not [do so] from their own, but come to this from his wickedness, when he hears toward the word: 'And you say in your mind: I shall ascend into heaven' (Ps 10:4) and the following. For no one else cast pride upon him, but he himself upon himself; therefore also no word...

For, as previously stated, the human [nature] entering in without the energy of virtue is most harmful, but with all things it is useful; which God also commanded like the manner of a good physician, providing a most useful drink for health, which when held together is effective, but when divided harms, just as it is previously stated regarding the so-called 'beast-like' [diet]. Such is what the Lord says he is teaching in the Gospels: 'Become wise as serpents and innocent as doves' (Matt 10:16).

But regarding these things, Adam says he blames the woman: 'The woman whom you gave with me, she gave to me from the tree and we ate' (Gen 3:12). Envy is a friend to malice, and it is the property of those who sin not to quickly confess the sin, but to divert the blame of the slip. For some think that men give their lives to fate from that [source] and are compelled toward sin, while others say that all things happen by chance and think that these things happen just so. But the first-formed [man], having heard the commandment, says: 'The woman whom you gave with me' (Gen 3:12).

It was necessary for him to understand that first, having received her from God, he also properly received her and that which is advantageous; then, he did not receive her as a teacher, but as one following him. And this we perceived in the fallen ones from the response of the Eve toward the serpent, speaking to him: 'We eat from the fruit of the tree of paradise, but from the fruit of the tree which is in the midst of the paradise God said: Do not eat of it, nor shall you touch it, lest you die' (Genesis 3:3); for God had not commanded concerning touching, but she, having learned this as if from Adam, was being taught to be more reverent, since, being weak, she heard from him not even to touch it. How then [can] the teacher and guide [be...] from the one being led into deception...

Those defending Adam argue from what was said to him: 'The woman whom you gave me with me' (Gen 3:12), for since he said she was given to him with him, knowing that she would be cast out due to disobedience, he accompanied her not to participate in transgression, but for her benefit; for often teachers sympathize with the weaker, so that through this they might work out a repentance for them.

And these things they hold from what is said by Paul, which leads to Christ and the Church: 'Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, came into transgression' (1 Tim 2:14). It is understood, being referred to the woman's church and to Adam's Christ, to preserve the chain of allegory and to avoid the possibility that the human race, from which the church is fulfilled, might have used the transgression as a cause for the descent of the Savior, so that he might use the economy, through which curse and sin came, not being these things, but having received them through us.

And the Lord God said to the woman: 'What is this that you have done?' and the woman said: 'The serpent deceived me and I ate' (Gen 3:13). Three persons are introduced by blame here: the man, the woman, and the serpent. And the man had an apology that the woman had become a hindrance to him in eating from the forbidden tree, from which he knew he was naked; but the woman blames the serpent, saying: 'The serpent deceived me and I ate'; for God also sought the cause of the slip from them; but such a question is not borne toward the serpent. For he did not have the cause of the evil to lay upon another, being himself her progenitor.

This also the Lord teaches in the Gospels, saying concerning him: 'When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, for he is a liar and his father is the father of lies' (John 8:44); that is, the father of lies; for the devil does not have a father according to those who act mythically. For no one else cast pride upon him, but he himself upon himself; therefore also no word...

God, being a source of goodness, calls us again after the mistakes, not omitting the perfect knowledge of the good from our reasoning, even if through sin we turn away from virtue. This God also does to Adam in the present, calling him while he is hiding, saying to him, 'Where are you?' (Genesis 3:9). Because it is to be learned from the Acts of the Apostles that whenever someone is appointed to a rank, it is called a place—just as when the apostles, desiring to raise up a disciple to stand in the place of Judas the traitor who had put forward Jesus, were lifting up a prayer to God, they were saying, 'You, Lord, know the hearts of all, reveal one to take the place of this ministry' (Acts 1:24). And it followed for Adam, having stepped out, the divine order that the suitable place of the rank would fall away; for he had been cast out from the paradise. And the 'Where are you?' (Genesis 3:9) might even be embarrassing; for [God says] 'I indeed placed you in virtue, but now where are you?' understanding this, he is ashamed.

And those who, understanding the incorporeal essence as the primary underlying substrate of the soul, and because of this, ought to consider her to be outside of every place, hear it embarrassingly, [as if God says] 'Where are you?' For it was necessary for a rebuke, which naturally from...

It becomes a benefit, combining discipline with mercy; for this reason it is said, 'And the Lord God called' (Gen 3:8). David also sings this, saying, 'I will sing to you of mercy and judgment, Lord' (Ps 89:13); for by joining the act of showing mercy with the act of judging, he shows a pattern of philanthropy. Let us also see the response: 'I heard your voice walking in the paradise' (Gen 3:8). For when someone, having become a sinner, prays for a brief perception to merely receive the understanding of God through creation—in which He walks, providing order to each of the existing things—then he turns back and recognizes that He surveys all things and governs them; thus, even through external observation, it happens. For when one beholds the sun's ordered course, the heavens' movement, the moon's changes, the stars' seasonal intervals, and reasons that the driver and commander of all this is the Creator of all things, walking among all, he hears the voice of God, not occurring by chance, but being impressed upon the intellect, that nothing escapes God, but all things are under His economy. And thus, being ashamed, he hides; for the one sinning, not having God before his eyes, sins.

Regarding perception, it is said: 'I heard your voice walking in the paradise and I was afraid, because I am naked' (Gen 3:10). For that very fear still holds a flash of how shameful and chastening vice is. He says that the cause of the fear is the nakedness, which comes from having lost virtue, which was a covering; for virtue is a divine garment. Thus also Paul exhorts: 'Put on the Lord Jesus' (Rom 13:14) and 'Put on the bowels of compassion' (Col 3:12), which is: be adorned in a merciful manner and in the Christ-like way of life; and again: 'Let us put on the armor of light' (Rom 13:12) to prepare ourselves to fight against the adversaries. Since, therefore, he was deprived of these garments because of the transgression, and was being reproved by his conscience, he did not have the boldness to gaze upon God; for this reason he says: 'I was afraid, because I am naked' (Gen 3:10); for just as one who has done absurd things, if he were to seek [to face] a ruler regarding what has been done, hides himself, so also Adam, who [did not]...

before: After Methuselah was born, Enoch found favor with God after two hundred and thirty years, and he fathered sons and daughters. And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years. And Enoch found favor with God, and he was not found, because God transferred him.

The Apostle, having received the word concerning Enoch, says in the Epistle to the Hebrews: 'By faith Enoch was transferred so as not to see death' (Heb 11:5). His life is described in a number of days, and having completed a year and a remainder, he was transferred, which one would logically consider to be a translation into better things, since he was promised the virtue which ought to exist in humans according to perfection and fullness. But his translation did not happen like that of other men; for the bodies of the others, remaining here and being dissolved, were separated from the souls; concerning this it is said that he was transferred, about which we understand that either he was taken up like Elijah or by some other way he was snatched into a divine place.

It is proper to observe here how what is said by Paul, 'And just as it is appointed for men to die once' (Heb 9:27), is made true. For if these, I say Elijah and Enoch, having been taken up, are to be with their thickest bodies even now and throughout the whole age, then the word of the wise and holy Paul concerning the necessity of all men dying is false. But it is not false. Therefore, what is set forth requires a theory, even if not in the way accustomed, that although other men have shared in death now, it must be understood that their mortal part is to be set aside according to the secret word of God, so that they might possess the fleshy life. For if the Savior is the 'firstborn from the dead' (Col 1:18), He would be the firstborn of these.

For it is undignified for such a word to be outside of them; furthermore, if they did not lay aside the fleshy life, as we have said, they would not have shared in the divine resurrection, by which from the dishonorable we shall all receive the body as honorable, from the glory as splendid, from the weak as powerful, from the psychic as spiritual. If one also reads the book of the Testament to a friend, he will know that he is said to be snatched into Paradise; and to know this, even if it is not from an irreproachable book, is not absurd. And there are those who [speak of] the translation by way of way...

They say it is so, according to which the Savior said to the disciples, 'You are no longer of this world, but I have chosen you' (John 15:19), effecting a transfer of election from the worldly things; and they receive another explicit thing constructed by this: 'We know that we have passed from death into life' (1 John 3:14). For those having passed from the death which follows through wickedness, we have been transferred unto the life which is from virtue.

This repayment suits not only Enoch, but all the saints; therefore, examine whether it is fitting to approve the former. And Noah was 500 years old, and Noah fathered three sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth. It is to be observed that he did not say at this point from how many years he began to father, but by chance he had three sons, not born at once. And it is also good that it is written that he had not fathered daughters, but sons, as a symbol showing that the righteous man is not a female-bearer, just as it has been written concerning Moses and Abraham; for these also did not have daughters.

For indeed someone is blessed, according to the Psalm, a father of well-born offspring, hearing: 'Blessed are you, and it shall be well with you. Your children like olive shoots around your table; thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord' (Psalm 128:3-4). But the daughters are perceived as symbols. Immediately also the tyrant Pharaoh, being fond of the males born by the Hebrews, destroys them, taking possession of the females. For those offspring of the soul that are well-born, those turning toward the things below strive to destroy, rejoicing in wealth and human things.

Immediately also the following explicitly teaches this: as a multitude became, daughters were born to them (Genesis 6:1). And it happened when men began to multiply on the earth, and daughters were born to them. The 'many' can also be applied to a multitude, over which especially it is most dominant, even regarding the Egyptians. For in the Exodus it is said: 'And the sons of Israel were fruitful and became Egyptians' (Exodus 1:7). But also the 'Many say to my soul' (Psalm 51:5) instead of 'Egyptians'; for words do not bring serious matters. And Paul, saying: 'For we are not as many who corrupt the word of the Lord' (2 Cor 2:17), shows those who are negligent. And also the...

The inner man is a gift from heaven, and it is fitting to seek God.

Regarding the things which are said, 'Many waters cannot quench love' (Song of Songs 8:7), being used as a symbol, one is not able to be overcome once by the opposing power, about which the saint cries, 'Save me from many waters' (Psalm 69:1), which leads to 'from the hand of strange sons' (Psalm 68:21), water meaning the strange sons. And again, 'If you pass through fire, flame shall not burn you, if through water, rivers shall not overwhelm you' (Isaiah 43:2), which is an athletic prize given to the just. And if someone took these things from the rivers of the sensible, it would not be a great thing not to be overwhelmed by the rivers of the sensible, with many and other evil things being expected of this; but it is a great thing not to be carried away by the streams of the opposing energies nor by the immeasurable wickedness of these, which is a reward becoming the just and a proper end.

Since, being presented through water, the rational animals show that by their own impulse and will the things in wickedness and the things in virtue have happened. For all things happened so that one might have virtue, but some did not preserve the given thing by their own slight deviation. Since God also made man good, but they themselves turned away from the goodness.

The deep, however, is deep water, of which there is no measure to be taken, the depth being made manifest by length and breadth. He says the Spirit hovers over the water; and if the simplest understanding were to fall [gap]... lying upon the immeasurable water and especially... since the Spirit [gap] with the senses...

With such discourses, he sows spiritual things many times, he who even now performs the movement. Therefore, it is preserved, for they did not make [something] of waters according to nature, but [something else].

The abyss would be the darkness of ignorance. A holy [thing] is brought over the [powers], spirits, principalities, thrones, lordships. 'God saw the waters, and they saw and were afraid' (Psalm 77:16). It is evident, however, that it is not about sensible waters, for he neither fears nor sees, for they are inanimate; for God sees [not with eyes] but understands with unmixed and pure [intellect].

Evil exists in [things] according to nature, but virtue exists part by part from [knowledge]. 'And God said, Let there be light, and there was light' (Genesis 1:3). What light is [there] with the luminaries, as in 'Praise him, sun, and moon, praise him, all you stars and light' (Psalm 148:3)? Perhaps it is not entirely irreconcilable to have the notion that before the sun there was some radiance, thinking that another light was to be. For they say that [it] was not yet defining [something] for us, but [it] appeared. Some radiance leaps forward, an external radiance of the sun, the form of sensible lights, as if rays of light.

before: “Behold, the fragrance of my son is as the fragrance of a full field which the Lord blessed” (Song of Solomon 4:12). He who conducts his cultivation well will hear, just as the bride: “A garden enclosed, my sister, a garden enclosed.” And “and it was so” and the following things are said for the sake of reciprocity. Genesis 1:12. And God saw that it was good. It is to be noted that, when two things have been commanded and have come to be, it is said as if they were one: “God saw that it was good.” For “God saw that it was good” is said toward the end and the purpose of the sequence; for the sake of men the vegetation sprouted and the other things. I say that what has the analogy in sensible things is good, how much more that which is in virtues and the harmony of a soul living well and choosing the excellent things according to reason and hastening toward the end of virtue. Genesis 1:14–19. And God said: “Let there be lights in the expanse of the heaven for the shining of the earth and for dividing between the day and between the night, and let them be for signs and for seasons and for days and for years, and let them be for shining in the expanse of the heaven so as to shine upon the earth”; and it was so, until it became the fourth day (Genesis 1:14-19).

Beginning the book, we say that God, being an active essence, simultaneously wills and is what he wills to be; for it is not possible for his activities to be prior to his existence, as is the case with human arts. For after the work is performed, the house is, and after the building, the house; for the house is not in the building, nor the ship in the shipbuilding; for these activities are measured by time. But God acts without time, leading toward the being which he wills; so therefore activity will not be following [something]. As soon as it was willed that the lights be, they are, and as soon as he willed the water to be gathered into one collection, the command was fulfilled, and in saying “Let there be an expanse”...

Hence, following this thought, […] concerning the six days we must understand as not taken for the sake of temporal extension, but of a logic proper to the creation of God and of the power of number. For six is the first of the perfect numbers: and they call perfect numbers those completed from their own parts — and there are only four from one to ten thousand. Six, then, is first: its half is three, its third two, its sixth one, which added together make six. Likewise with twenty-eight: its half is fourteen, its fourth seven, its seventh four, its fourteenth two, its twenty-eighth one, which again added together make twenty-eight. And besides these there are two others; but if you add others besides the perfect ones, they fall short or exceed, as must be observed in the case of eight: half four, fourth two, eighth one, which again added together bring a lesser number. And twelve added together exceeds: its half six, its third four, its fourth three, its sixth two, its twelfth one. Those concerned with these things call the deficient ones “defective,” the excessive ones “overfull,” and the ones completed from themselves “perfect.”

It was fitting, then, for God, making a perfect creation, to bring it into being in the first perfect number — not that we should altogether say that six days elapsed while the sun circled six times (for the sun had not yet come to be in the first three), but that the number six was taken for the sake of logic and harmony. Moses himself sets forth this thought exactly, making the recapitulation of what happened, saying: “This is the book of the generation of heaven and earth, when it came to be, in the day God made heaven and earth” (Gen 2:4). For altogether neither did heaven and earth come to be in a day, but “in the beginning,” nor did all things come into being in one day, but it is clear that, at once […].

before: It was said previously regarding certain cages, machines, and hooks for men. These things happen such that even the most fearsome, like the lion and the leopard, whose nature is most wild, are often subjected to the hand of man. And thus the rule over them exists, God having provided this to them.

But it is necessary to know that the manner of rule exists in different ways. One rule is a legal supervision of both the ruler and the ruled; for the law gives authority and rule to the ruler and to the subject, so that in the same way the ruler rules and the subject is subjected, the law directing that it should be done thus. Otherwise, a teacher rules over students, and differently, a master over slaves, and a general over an army. Thus, man rules over irrational animals in different ways, as has been said: in some ways as domestic, in others according to their wild nature; for not all are edible, but some are already for medicinal use and for another contributing need, which the physiologist will find.

Furthermore, to these belongs the [word]: 'And God said, Behold, I have given you every seed-bearing plant spreading seed, which is upon the face of all the earth' (Gen 1:29). For God gave authority and knowledge, so that man might know which of those upon the earth is useful for food, and which for medicine, and which for another need. But there is a different nature to these: some are trees, some are vegetables, and some are grasses, and above all, some are edible and some are good for another use.

The need of these should not be ignored according to the command before this—when God said, 'Let the earth sprout herb-bearing seed-bearing plant according to its kind' (Gen 1:11), He adds, 'and a fruitful tree producing fruit' (Genesis 1:11), because the trees differ from the herb, calling them 'fruitful trees'—not only does man exercise authority over those resulting from agriculture, but also over their materials which he neither sows nor cultivates, as he has different needs from these; for He does not make these things portable throughout the inhabited places, but it is evident that for the necessity of men, every plant has become a sprout; for all things are made for their use.

The providential character of God over all things is signaled by His declaration: "It shall be for food to you, and to all the beasts of the earth, and to all the fowls of the heaven" (Genesis 9:3). For it is fitting that He who cares for men should also provide for the animals that have become necessary and useful to them, and for other things useful to them; for indeed, not according to the prior logic of irrational things, but indeed through man, He has fashioned His providence. God saw all things again to be good, for they bring forth [fruit]: "And God saw all that He had made, and behold, it was very good" (Genesis 1:31). Before this, however, the word had praised each of the things coming into being by saying, "And God saw that it was good" (Genesis 1:25, 1:31) or "good"; but now it is stated with certainty, "very good," because of the harmony and concord of all things.

Let what is said be clear through an example. One who wishes to assemble a dance selects the best dancers for each part, so that nothing is lacking for their specific task; if, moreover, these are brought together for that which has prepared them, he will find the work resulting from their concord to be exceedingly and superlatively beautiful, which is not possible to result from a single person alone. One might also find this in a military camp: for it is necessary that there be a best spearman, a best archer, a best general, and a best counselor, so that when the time comes, the work of all being joined together may show the magnitude of praise, being referred to a single purpose. The word teaches that all things are "very good" (Genesis 1:31) by showing their interconnectedness, their proportion, their harmony, and their ordered state, and even the unshakable stability of opposites; which, as was said before, is not perceived by the senses, but is judged by the Word. This is the explicit statement; since we have already spoken regarding the preceding words and the induction, now this must be done. before: Having used the fifty-fold, he rose up and spoke of other things, but they did not understand that they had achieved such a thing not by using sword or any defense, but having called upon God himself and having received him leaning toward help through prayer; to whom, if they had made the prayer from anger, God would not have attended through his own exhortation, as it is fitting for the one praying to lift up holy hands without anger or disputations.

Therefore, from the virtue of the saints, the pretenders, desiring to hide their own faults by scattering leaves, think they are making a defense, just as it happened even regarding the first humans. To those using such a purpose, the Lord symbolically rebukes through the fig tree in the Gospels, having come to it and finding nothing but leaves, saying, 'No more shall fruit come from you for an age' (Matthew 21:19). And we do not say that the rebuke was spoken to the fig tree itself; for the sensible fig tree did not bear fruit not because of its own cause. But it is also said regarding Israel having fallen into impiety: 'There is no cluster in the vines, nor figs in the fig trees.' They therefore scattered fig leaves as a plausible defense, as has been said, providing it, but the word is not following the form of the history.

For since paradise was introduced and nakedness and, after this persuasion, knowledge, the word, using the cover from leaves, says it is being made for the subject of the narration according to the custom of the God-breathed Scripture. For often the soul is called at times a vine, at times a sheep, at times a bride in the divine instruction, and the word proceeds accordingly to each one after the other. For when he posits her as a vine, saying, 'A vine flourishing in Israel' (Hosea 10:1), then he calls the teacher-farmers and the attackers foxes; for 'catch for us foxes, even the little foxes that spoil the vineyards' (Song of Solomon 2:15); but when [she is] a sheep...

He names the teachers shepherds and those who turn away wolves and lions; it has been said: 'Israel, a wandering sheep, lions drove him away' (cf. Jeremiah 50:17/55:23). But also when he calls her a bride, he names the one leading into the truth a bridegroom and the one harming an adulterer; and all these things, even if they are different names, regarding the soul, are considered appropriate and fitting to the Divine Spirit in thought, not because this is a sheep or a bride or a vine.

Consequently, therefore, a memory of paradise having occurred, through the form of the word, he mentioned leaves, which those having fallen from virtue scattered according to the aforementioned understanding. And these themselves also heard the Lord God walking in the paradise. And before the transgression, he was not walking around them outside of them, but was with them.

For of the one guarding virtue and being in it, this is appropriate, as to say: 'I have set the Lord always before me, for he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken' (Ps 16:8), and 'But I am with you always' (Mt 28:20). And of the man being with God, and God being with him: it has been said: 'Draw near to God and he will draw near to you' (Jas 4:8); but when some turn away from him, they hear: 'They went astray from me, and I will go to them in angry wrath' (Hos 8:1).

And just as the one leaving the sun and closing his eyes does not do anything to make the sun less—for it remains as it was, shining—so the one leaving God works harm upon himself; and he leaves him not as if in a place, but turning away from virtue, as those about whom it has been said: 'God will cast them off, because they did not listen to him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Dt 32:19); for because they themselves did not listen, he cast them off. Since therefore even these through the transgression turned away from him, and he himself has become distant from them, yet because he walks through his own goodness, providing perception...

before: They present their offerings as thanksgiving, doing so naturally; but those who use them carelessly, as if keeping the precious things for themselves and offering the cheap ones, have made a poor choice. Since Israel does this very thing, the prophetic word says rebukingly and admonishingly: 'If you bring a blind man for sacrifice, is it not bad? And if you bring a lame or sick man, is it not bad? Bring him to your leader' (Malachi 1:8).

But also Ananias and Sapphira in the Acts of the Apostles, when many were offering for the needs of those in need, they themselves received the price of a field, from which, having decided upon it, they brought the half and the other half making a poor choice, which the apostle's spokesman, inspired by the Spirit, rebuking said: 'Was it not still yours, and was it not under your control when you sold it? Why did you dare to do this in your heart?' (Acts 5:3-4). This also was said to Cain by God: 'Why are you so troubled, and why is your face downcast? If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned' (Genesis 4:6).

For all sin as they bring to God as a needy person, ignoring what was said in the Psalms toward Him, the God: 'Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?' (Psalm 50:13) and also: 'Mine are all the beasts of the field, cattle on the mountains and oxen' (Psalm 50:10). For all that you have in abundance from me, I also have all things, so that one not in need did not command, but rather from these, using them symbolically, it is fitting to use virtue not carelessly, but perfectly and completely.

Furthermore, in order that the evil may not advance, it is exhorted to be at rest from it, so that by rubbing against it one might not work up a worse sorrow. In this way it is also said to Zion, being moved disorderly—for such is the name—'Stand up, you, Zion' (Isaiah 62:1). Since the rational animal is active, either working out evil or virtue, in a manner of speaking,

When one does evil, it is appropriate for him to stand against this, so that virtue may find the space that is becoming. This indeed David advises: 'Turn away from evil' (Psalm 34:14), saying, 'and do good' (Psalm 34:14). 'Be still' (Genesis 4:7), therefore, he says, do not progress through evil; do not consider through negligence as if your sacrifice was not properly received. For many, often stumbling themselves and for this reason not having God as a co-worker, are displeased with providence, which God prevents in Cain, saying: 'Be still' (Genesis 4:7).

And also the 'his turning toward you and you shall turn him back' (Genesis 4:7) comes, teaching that whatever is offered to God not according to what is becoming, these things are not offered to him, but belong to the Giver, turning back toward him because of not having found a place in God. So also those providing alms for the sake of being seen by men withhold their own reward, having nothing from God; for they did not do this with a divine purpose. The whole discourse of the word is most useful for character, and thus being taken simply, it teaches sincerely regarding offerings and not to do them carelessly; and since we lead the aforementioned into the modes of the soul in the instances of errors, it is necessary even now to do this.

The word of God, existing according to common concepts and being present to the conscience, paternally reproves those stumbling, which is also presented now. For the hypocrites, insofar as to show virtue for honor, even if they do not choose it, seem to do something right; because they use a bad division, the one moving from the depth of the intention toward their own pleasures, the other shaping themselves to make the gift of outward appearance through God, it is expected they are not acceptable, cleaning the outside of the cup (Matthew 23:25) and surrounding themselves outwardly with the skin of a sheep, but being wolves within, snatching (Matthew 7:15); to such ones, reproving...

Whether therefore men are being driven by demons having taken daughters, or, as is previously rendered, the angels of desirable sensations, the Spirit does not remain in these. And if anyone brings an objection as to how the pre-existing souls desired bodies, of which they did not know, it must be said to whom that desiring is often said not strictly as desiring that toward which their actions lead. before: It has been completed, rather than being filled; it lies there. For it is not their existence that has been completed, but their making, just as we say also concerning the poetic arts, which bring the end through their activities, saying that the ship or the house has been completed.

Thus the heaven has been completed, having received its proper harmony, which received its fullness from both the firmament and the luminaries and also from the stars, and the earth from both the animals and the various plants. And when each of them had become, the 'has been completed' did not fit; but now, having received the concord and the harmony of all things, the 'The heaven and the earth and all their world were completed' follows.

And it is said that the world of the earth and its fullness according to what is said: 'The earth is the Lord's and its fullness' (Ps 24:1). Because even the variety of the heaven is called a world, Moses himself says concerning them in his words: 'Not looking up to the heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, all the world of the heaven, being led astray, you shall worship them' (Deut 4:19), who through the position which was set by God, demonstrate beauty, some by moving in these circulations, others to be with these, some making their motion in a straight line, and others in an arc.

An army of heaven, therefore, because of the arrangement, has been said according to what has been said: 'Whose hands made all the host of heaven' (Job 38:7). Concerning which, those who have not understood well have erred, introducing fate and setting all things by necessity, defining the stars to be determining the poetic lives of men and the things happening to others, who, for a sign, if not for the doing, have been set according to also... concerning those having happened on the fourth day, we demonstrated the 'Let them be for signs and for seasons and for months and for years' (Gen 1:14), setting forth as if human life has not been compelled by the stars. For those escaping life through war and universal accidents are not under one formation. And moreover, the argument of fate is more strongly overturned.

From the laws: all Jews, having reached the eighth day from birth, are circumcised, and they receive the trial of iron even from the sprouts [infants], and no one could say how all at once they cast [the foreskin] off within a single hour, almost everywhere on earth and every day as Jews are born; but they say that even certain Ethiopians have the membranes of the genitals removed at the same time as birth, and even these do not all have their birth at once; and altogether the various customs and laws according to the nations negate fate. If this does not fit according to fate, much more do the things of choice. For if fate leads the happening by necessity, and choice has power over the possible things, fate will not be about these things. For virtue and vice have benefited or harmed the one possessing them, and each of those doing [actions] is blamed because of the bad habits, or praised for acting rightly; but the things happening by necessity [omitted]... no one accepts or blames the one doing something by necessity. Furthermore, if the laws are from fate, and those not obeying these are not from fate, it seems to negate and overturn fate itself. Significant, then, are the stars, not as makers, but signifying the weather or pestilential occurrences or something else that seems to the one foreseeing, and these things are about this.

Let us return to the thing set forth from the beginning: 'And God finished on the sixth day his works, which he made' (Gen 2:2), which indicates as if the completion is about the only ones which he has made. For there are works which have not yet happened, which were foretold as being to come, such as the resurrection of the dead and entirely those things which are to be according to providence, which happen in their own sequence from God. So the addition 'of the works which he made' is appropriately placed. It is also necessary to contemplate this, that God did not 'rest' (Gen 2:2) in the seventh without having acted, for already all things were completed; but he 'blessed' (Gen 2:3) only the seventh day and sanctified it, and the saying leads to this: 'That in it he rested from all his works, which God began to make' (Gen 2:2). 'Which he began'—for it is not the beginning of all the works...
after: It has been completed, rather than being filled; it lies there. For it is not their existence that has been completed, but their making, just as we say also concerning the poetic arts, which bring the end through their activities, saying that the ship or the house has been completed.

Thus the heaven has been completed, having received its proper harmony, which received its fullness from both the firmament and the luminaries and also from the stars, and the earth from both the animals and the various plants. And when each of them had become, the 'has been completed' did not fit; but now, having received the concord and the harmony of all things, the 'The heaven and the earth and all their world were completed' follows.

And it is said that the world of the earth and its fullness according to what is said: 'The earth is the Lord's and its fullness' (Ps 24:1). Because even the variety of the heaven is called a world, Moses himself says concerning them in his words: 'Not looking up to the heaven and seeing the sun and the moon and the stars, all the world of the heaven, being led astray, you shall worship them' (Deut 4:19), who through the position which was set by God, demonstrate beauty, some by moving in these circulations, others to be with these, some making their motion in a straight line, and others in an arc.

An army of heaven, therefore, because of the arrangement, has been said according to what has been said: 'Whose hands made all the host of heaven'. Concerning which, those who have not understood well have erred, introducing fate and setting all things by necessity, defining the stars to be determining the poetic lives of men and the things happening to others, who, for a sign, if not for the doing, have been set according to also... concerning those having happened on the fourth day, we demonstrated the 'Let them be for signs and for seasons and for months and for years' (Gen 1:14), setting forth as if human life has not been compelled by the stars. For those escaping life through war and universal accidents are not under one formation. And moreover, the argument of fate is more strongly overturned.

From the laws: all Jews, having reached the eighth day from birth, are circumcised, and they receive the trial of iron even from the sprouts [infants], and no one could say how all at once they cast [the foreskin] off within a single hour, almost everywhere on earth and every day as Jews are born; but they say that even certain Ethiopians have the membranes of the genitals removed at the same time as birth, and even these do not all have their birth at once; and altogether the various customs and laws according to the nations negate fate. If this does not fit according to fate, much more do the things of choice. For if fate leads the happening by necessity, and choice has power over the possible things, fate will not be about these things. For virtue and vice have benefited or harmed the one possessing them, and each of those doing [actions] is blamed because of the bad habits, or praised for acting rightly; but the things happening by necessity [omitted]... no one accepts or blames the one doing something by necessity. before: [...of] the fish of the sea and the winged ones of the heaven and the beasts and all the earth and all the creeping things creeping upon the earth. And God made the man; according to the image of God He made him, male and female He made them. And God blessed them, saying: 'Increase and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it, and rule over the fish of the sea and the winged ones of the heaven and all the beasts and all the earth and all the creeping things creeping upon the earth' (Gen 1:28).

The word 'man' signifies also the composite living thing which is composed of soul and body, and especially the soul. Therefore, the wise Peter the apostle calls the hidden part of the heart 'man', and the blessed Paul: 'For I consent according to the law of God according to the inner man' (Rom 7:22), that is, according to the mind, according to the soul. But when it is said: 'There was a certain man in the land of Assyria' (Job 1:1), and: 'It happened when many men began to become' (Genesis 6:1), it signifies the common [meaning]. If therefore we take the explicit [meaning], the composite man signifies the 'And God said: Let us make man' (Gen 1:26).

And not only regarding the composite, but even regarding the visible and perceptible, that is, the body, the blessed Paul intends to extend the name of man, saying: 'Even if our outward man is being destroyed, but the inward is being renewed day by day' (2 Cor 4:16). And according to a first imposition, each of us was composed of soul and body, but there are those who say that man is composed of three, of soul and body and spirit, which they construct by joining themselves to the apostolic saying which says: 'And the God of peace sanctify you completely, and your whole spirit and soul and body' (1 Thess 5:23), not following [the idea] that it must be said concerning the Holy Spirit in order to be whole, which is not even destined to come into weakness. Therefore, they produce another proof from a different saying having this: 'The Spirit itself bears witness with our spirit' (Rom 8:16); for they say our spirit is a different spirit from the Holy Spirit, being witnessed by the Holy Spirit when it is well. And that from Daniel: 'Spirits and souls of the righteous, bless the Lord' (Dan 4:35).

They think it is a mere assistant. But those who do not want there to be anything other than the spirit besides the soul say that it signifies the will through the spirit, or that he has shown even the soul by the designation of the spirit. But those renewing this argument say that, having used a connective conjunction, even in 'spirits and souls of the righteous' (cf. Heb 11:35), he shows the soul to be something other than the spirit.

And as a constructive argument for the composition of man from soul and body, they produce that which is said in the Gospel, broken out: 'Do not fear those who kill the body but are not able to kill the soul; but fear him who is able to destroy both soul and body in hell' (Matthew 10:28). And if it is the case that men kill one thing and not the other, then the body and the soul are two. We say, therefore, man and the body only, but not simply, but man with an addition; and the soul alone is man not simply, but man within; and the composite is man simply, without anything added.

Let it therefore be sought here concerning what is said regarding God of all things: 'Let us make man according to an image and in our likeness' (Gen 1:26). The man has not become according to an image of God in the composite sense; for God is not man-shaped. And the divine teaching confirms this; for it is said that God is spirit and light (1 John 1:5), and light and spirit do not have the form of man.

But the Scripture also discusses God having seven eyes, seeing all the earth (Zechariah 4:10), while man has two; so therefore the man will not be found to be according to the image of God in this way of our seeing. But these things we say not as if God has seven sensible eyes, but we are investigating how man is according to the image and likeness of God; for the Word has shown his perfect contemplative power through the seven, and through the virtues which the number seven has, as has already been foretold.

Again, God is said to have wings, just as the holy one says: 'In the shelter of your wings you will protect me' (Ps 17:8); but man is a wingless animal, and the wingless is not able to have the image and likeness of God, not through sensible things received by us, but through intuitions surpassing and carrying those who desire this upward. It must therefore be investigated how man is according to the image and likeness of God.
